Occasionally, I update an indicator I call the Walmart Recession Signal (WRS). Recessions are typically felt first, and ultimately more emphatically, by lower income individuals than by the wealthier parts of the economy. Walmart specifically caters to the lower income distribution and thereby could provide an early read on economic stress. From 1990 to mid-2005, the WRS is defined as the ratio of Walmart’s stock to the S&P 500 Retail Stock Price Index. Since July 2025, the WRS compares Walmart’s stock price performance to a group of stocks whose businesses are tied to the wealthiest parts of the economy – the S&P Global Luxury Index. As economic activity slows and recession risk builds, retailing purchasing patterns tend to gravitate toward discounters like Walmart and away from overall or luxury retailors. Consequently, a rise in the WRS could warn of a potential recession or at least a significant economic slowdown.

# Executive Summary 6Speculative data center debt is being repackaged and sold to pension and retirement funds, university endowments, and other institutional investors in a manner eerily reminiscent of the subprime bubble. Private equity ffrms have purchased life insurers and loaded them with risky debt, exposing policyholders and the public to losses and raising the threat of ffnancial contagion. Rather than address these mounting risks, the Trump administration and federal ffnancial regulators are ripping up regulatory guardrails and exacerbating the harms a potential crisis would cause. They must dramatically reverse course to reduce the likelihood of disaster. Regulators, Congress, and state policymakers should instead act swiftly to shine a light on the AI industry’s murky ffnances, stop contributing to the infiation of the bubble with subsidies and regulatory giveaways, better protect working people’s retirement savings from outsized risk exposure, and strengthen the resilience of the ffnancial system to protect households’ economic security and the broader economy’s stability. This report’s purpose is not to predict a speciffc sequence of events or portray an economic crisis as inevitable. It is instead to argue that the ingredients for a serious crisis are in place, explain why inaction regarding the growing risks would be a dangerous mistake, and describe the steps that policymakers should take to mitigate the growing threats to economic stability. Time is running short. 

# Executive Summary 

# The artificial intelligence (AI) boom represents one of the largest speculative frenzies in history. The ten most valuable U.S. companies are all tech giants. And most U.S. tech giants — including Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle, and SpaceX — are at the center of a multi-trillion-dollar spending spree on data centers and related infrastructure to train and run generative AI models. With tech companies spending drastically more on AI infrastructure than they are earning from selling AI products and services, however, even the biggest AI companies have begun borrowing heavily to cover AI’s extraordinarily high costs. That skyrocketing debt means that AI giants will need to earn multiples more in revenue than they are earning now to cover their spending. If the AI industry can’t pay back its mounting debts, a financial crash could follow — and it could spread well beyond the tech sector. 7

PART I: BUBBLE TROUBLES 

With more than a third of the S&P 500’s valuation residing in a handful of tightly interconnected tech companies laden with trillions of dollars in debt, the AI bubble is unique in recent history in its size, scope, and risk. • As of September 2026, the U.S. stock market is: o More overvalued by most traditional metrics than it has been since at least the peak of the dot-com bubble (see Figure ES-1). o More concentrated in its largest companies (see Figure ES-2) than it has been since the 1960s. o More concentrated in a single sector (see Figure ES-3) than it has been since the 1890s. o Larger relative to the total economy (see Figure ES-4) than it has ever been. • AI companies are spending over a trillion dollars in 2026 on generative AI infrastructure but bringing in only a small fraction of that amount in sales of generative AI products and services. • To cover that gap, AI companies have taken on enormous quantities of increasingly risky debt and are using dubious accounting tactics, including the extensive use of circular financing arrangements to inflate earnings and shell companies to hide off-balance-sheet debt. • These factors, together with other pockets of risk building up in the economy, mean that the odds of a deep and severe AI crash are rapidly increasing.

PART II: HOW AN AI CRASH COULD START AND SPREAD 

The risk is rising that AI companies will be unable to meet their fast-growing debt obligations. Regardless of where market stress originates, the industry’s extensive circular financial arrangements mean that turmoil could easily spread and devastate the entire tech sector. • AI companies need to quickly achieve immense profits to pay their mounting debts, but several forces are making it difficult for them to do so (see Figure ES-5): o Questionable demand for generative AI products and services o Fierce competition among model developers o Persistent high costs, resource constraints, and community opposition to data centers • The industry’s smaller and more precarious players are most vulnerable to these forces, but the various players in the AI ecosystem are deeply interconnected, as the complex corporate arrangements for a massive data center in Abilene, Texas illustrate (see Figure ES-6). As a result, a crash affecting any one part of the industry would likely spread. • Even the tech giants would be vulnerable to a deep AI downturn because of their huge amounts of debt (most of it hidden off their balance sheets), weakening cash flows (see Figure ES-7), and revenues that appear to be artificially inflated by the AI industry’s web of circular financing.

PART III: WHY AN AI CRASH WOULD POSE SERIOUS MACROECONOMIC RISKS 

The outsized role of the tech sector in equity and credit markets means that any crash originating in the tech sector would be exceedingly difficult to contain. • The high levels of leverage (see Figure ES-8) and the prominent role of passive index funds in the current market could amplify an AI market crash and accelerate its spread to the rest of the stock market. • Both private investment funds and life insurers have significant exposure to AI-linked debt, including Big Tech’s huge pile of off-balance-sheet debt (see Figure ES-9), and numerous touchpoints with the U.S. banking system, providing paths for the widespread amplification of financial stress in the event of an AI crash. Commercial banks’ own exposure to AI-linked debt and ties to the rest of the shadow banking system increase the risk of contagion. • With more Americans’ wealth tied up in the stock market than ever before (see Figure ES-10), an AI crash could destroy trillions (and perhaps tens of trillions) of dollars in wealth, wiping out millions of Americans’ pensions and retirement savings and threatening downward spirals in the real economy. • An AI crash would have a serious negative effect on economic investment as well, particularly because many specialized AI chips and data centers could become stranded, toxic assets. • The economic threat comes not from any one of these factors, but from the fact that the economy would have to navigate all these challenges in the aftermath of an AI crash.

PART IV: WHAT CAN BE DONE? 

The AI bubble poses serious threats to economic security and financial stability. But, while the threat is grave, there are steps that policymakers can and should take to lessen the severity of a potential AI crash and limit the harm an AI crash would inflict on everyday people. Unfortunately, the Trump administration and federal regulators are instead weakening 

safeguards intended to bolster our financial stability — lowering capital standards, increasing everyday investors’ exposure to risk, reducing market transparency, and slashing oversight and risk management requirements — even as financial risks are fast accumulating. What’s more, tax subsidies and federal tax breaks for data center construction (see ES-11) represent a not-insignificant amount of public dollars being thrown into the growing bubble. In addition to reversing those dangerous policy changes, federal regulators, Congress, and state and local governments should swiftly take proactive steps to: • Demand true financial transparency across the entire AI ecosystem, including the AI infrastructure buildout. • Close statutory and regulatory loopholes that enable deceptive accounting and financial practices across the industry. • Deter further reckless lending and speculative investments that threaten to transfer downside AI investment risk from wealthy insiders to everyday investors and retirement savers. • Strengthen the regulation and supervision of the AI industry’s Wall Street financiers — banks and shadow banks alike. In the event of an AI bubble-induced financial crisis: • The federal government must refuse to bail out AI firms and financiers who profited from the AI bubble. • Congress and the executive must prioritize the recovery and protection of workers and families by directing federal assistance to workers, households, and communities harmed by the crisis. • AI firms, Wall Street financiers, and executives across both industries must be investigated for their roles in the AI bubble’s inflation and held accountable for any and all unlawful activities. After any such crisis, policymakers should focus on reforming the financial system to prevent a recurrence, including by establishing strong safeguards that support the movement of capital towards productive ends and guarantee economic security for the many.

# Introduction 12 

# Introduction 

John Kenneth Galbraith’s The Great Crash, 1929 is one of the great works of economic history and analysis. Though it was written more than 70 years ago about events nearly 100 years ago, it remains strikingly salient. The rapid technological change of the late 19th and ear-ly 20th centuries created the largest and most valuable corporations the world had yet seen. During the Roaring Twenties, new technologies like radio and aviation captivat-ed investors who saw the potential for further technological transformation. With Corporate America promising a high-tech future marked by unprecedented prosperity, investors tried to grab a slice of that future by pouring money into the stock market as never before, driving it to levels that became increasingly difficult to justify in light of the com-panies’ underlying earnings. After the economy wobbled in the summer and early fall of 1929, however, investors lost their nerve, and the U.S. stock market experienced what remains the most devastating crash in its history. Galbraith argued that, severe as it was, the stock market crash alone did not lead to the Great Depression. Rather, the crash exposed and amplified other weaknesses in the economy that, together with the stock market rout, sent the U.S. economy into its darkest era. In the final chapter of The Great Crash , Galbraith focused on five weaknesses in particular: • “The bad distribution of income,” which made the economy heavily dependent on spending by the wealthy. • “The bad corporate structure,” particularly fragile, overleveraged arrangements where a single company’s failure to pay its bills could impose heavy losses on several other companies. • “The bad banking structure” in the form of interconnected financial institutions making risky loans in a manner that left them vulnerable to cascading bank runs. • “The dubious state of the foreign balance,” that is, an unequal balance of trade. • “The poor state of economic intelligence,” particularly policymakers who fundamentally misunderstood the nature and scale of the economic challenges before them and spent their time obsessing over shrinking the government rather than addressing the growing threat to the economy. 1Ninety-seven years after the crash, history is rhyming. Investors are once again captivated by promises of a technological revolution and are pouring money into the stock market. Thanks to an enormous bubble focused on the AI-obsessed tech industry, the U.S. stock market is, by most metrics, even frothier and more untethered from economic fundamentals than it was in 1929. 2 Each of the five macroeconomic weaknesses that Galbraith highlight-ed in The Great Crash has an eerie echo today: • Income and wealth inequality now matches or exceeds, depending on the measure, the levels from the Roaring Twenties. 3• Complex, opaque, and fragile corporate arrangements have become endemic, particularly through the AI industry’s extensive circular financing deals 4 and the precarious financing structures at the base of the multi-trillion-dollar data center boom. 5• Banks are bigger and more interconnected than ever, and much lending activity now occurs in the opaque, uninsured, and teetering realm of private credit, which has experienced the equivalent of bank runs in recent months. 6• The U.S. suffers from a deep imbalance of trade; today it is a trade deficit whereas a century ago it was a trade surplus, but a serious imbalance in either direction can amplify economic stress. 7• Policymakers, ideologically wedded to the belief that the greatest threat to the economy is regulation rather than reckless lending and speculation, are making things worse rather than better, with the Federal Reserve pushing to loosen bank capital requirements and the Trump administration moving to open workers’ 401(k)s to risky private credit and make financial markets less transparent. 8As if these were not enough, the current economic land-scape contains hazardous features that were either absent or not as prominent a century ago. Today’s stock market is larger than it has ever been as a percentage of GDP, and more Americans’ wealth is tied up in stocks than ever before. The stock market today is not only overvalued by traditional metrics; a historically disproportionate share of its value is tied up in a handful of tightly interconnected companies from the same industry. Those interconnected companies have taken on trillions of dollars’ worth of debt, much of it hidden off their balance sheets and distributed throughout shadow banks and institutional investors that have numerous connections to the commercial banks at the heart of the financial system. 13 

Because of these factors, the economy would be danger-ously exposed if the AI market fails to fulfill the extraordi-nary expectations that Silicon Valley and Wall Street have set for it. With tech companies spending drastically more on AI infrastructure than they are earning from selling AI products and services, the risk of an AI crash is increasing by the day. Given the outsized role that the AI industry plays in both equity and credit markets, such a crash could have impacts that go well beyond the AI industry — and well beyond those of a typical stock market crash. As it stands, regulators, markets, and finance experts alike seem almost cavalier about these mounting risks. The rea-sons for their lack of concern vary. Many in the tech indus-try and Wall Street argue that the market is not overvalued or headed for a correction at all. Despite the AI industry’s dubious finances, 9 they see not a bubble but an investment “super-cycle” that will lead to immense economic growth. 10 Some observers acknowledge that there is a bubble but ar-gue that if it bursts, only the tech industry’s weaker players would be at risk; the Big Tech giants would survive and the data centers they are building will, they claim, return value for years to come. 11 Others acknowledge that even the tech giants could be at risk in a steep enough downturn but posit that any crash would stay mostly contained to the tech sec-tor without spilling over to the financial system or broader economy. 12 Still others believe the usual monetary and fiscal policy toolkit could defuse a crisis before it spirals, implying that urgent action to prevent a crisis is not necessary. 13 This report explains why we believe such views to be too sanguine. The issue is not whether AI is or will be transformative. After all, radio and aviation did revolutionize our economy and society. But when it became clear that the returns would take far longer to materialize than investors and lenders expected, 14 the early waves of investors were crushed, and they eventually dragged the economy down with it, devastating the lives of tens of millions of workers and consumers. To be sure, the purpose of this report is not to predict a specific sequence of events or to convince readers that another Great Crash, much less another Great Depression, is the inevitable result of the fast-accumulating econom-ic risks. It is, rather, to argue that the ingredients for a severe economic crisis are in place, explain why excuses for inaction have become untenable, describe the steps that policymakers should take to defuse the growing threats to economic stability, and lay out some initial principles for responding to an AI crash. In so doing, we describe and explore various scenarios for how the bursting of the AI bubble could start and how its effects might spread. The risks are numerous and complex, and entire reports could (and should) be written analyzing many of the issues discussed in greater depth and detail. This report provides an overview, presenting the issues and risks in an order intended to enable readers to see not only their scale, but how they relate to each other and could make the burst-ing of the AI bubble difficult to contain if policymakers do not act decisively. Part I explores the characteristics of the AI boom that pose increasing and potentially systemic risks to the finan-cial system and economy. It analyzes the unprecedented scale of the AI bubble, the deep interconnectedness of the companies at the bubble’s epicenter, and the dubi-ous tactics that AI companies have adopted to present a misleading picture of the industry’s financial health. It also provides an overview of the other trouble spots in the fi-nancial system and economy that an AI market rout could expose or exacerbate. Part II analyzes the forces that will make it extremely challenging for the AI industry to pay its fast-mounting debts and explains that those forces mean that a crash would threaten not just the newer and weaker AI compa-nies, but, due to the AI ecosystem’s interconnectedness, the tech sector as a whole. Part III explains how a sufficiently severe AI market reversal could spiral into a severe economic crisis by triggering a broader stock market crash, damaging the financial system, and creating negative feedback loops in the real economy as businesses and consumers pull back on spending and investment. Part IV discusses steps that policymakers should take now to reduce the likelihood and severity of a dangerous AI crash and lays out some principles to guide action during and after such a crash to minimize the potential harm to the real economy and to working people. The AI bubble poses serious economic risks that are rising rapidly. But, disturbingly, federal policymakers are taking steps that make a crisis more likely and its consequences likely more severe. Time is running out to reverse course and head off a potential economic crisis on a scale the United States has not experienced in nearly a century. 14 

# Bubble troubles PART ONE 15 

# Part I: Bubble troubles 

The AI bubble is unprecedented in its size, its scope, and the degree to which it involves massive, tightly linked corporations, which have resorted to massive borrow-ing and dubious accounting to fuel their spending spree (Section A). Worse, the bubble is inflating in a climate rife with other significant economic trouble spots that would likely be exposed in an AI crash, including the precarious private credit sector, speculative cryptocurrency markets, and weaknesses arising from the AI industry’s voracious appetite for crucial resources (Section B). 

A. THE HISTORIC SCALE AND DUBIOUS ECONOMICS OF THE AI BUBBLE 

Nearly $33 trillion in market value has been added to the S&P 500 since ChatGPT’s release in late 2022, with the vast majority going to shares in companies whose futures are tethered to the AI boom. 15 

The money flooding into AI stocks has resulted in an overvalued market that is more concentrated in its larg-est companies than it has been since the 1960s, more concentrated in a single sector than it has been since the 1890s, and larger relative to the total economy than it has ever been. (Subsection 1).

1. The stock market: Overvalued, overconcentrated, and oversized a. The stock market is historically overvalued 

The stock market reaching new all-time highs, as it has repeatedly over the last few years, may seem like a welcome sight — and when stock prices reflect drivers of real economic growth, it is. But when share prices rise far above what companies’ economic fundamentals justify, they are a sign of a speculative bubble. Today, a wide variety of metrics show that the current U.S. stock market is overvalued to a historic degree, with several overvaluation signals approaching or exceeding their all-time highs. The Cyclically Adjusted Price to Earnings (CAPE) ratio is one such signal. The CAPE ratio compares the value of S&P 500 stocks to companies’ average profits over the preceding 10 years. 16 The higher the ratio, the more expensive large corporations’ stocks are relative to their underlying profits. 2. Data center arithmetic: Too much spending + Too little revenue = Skyrocketing debt 

The stratospheric stock-market valuations of AI-linked tech companies are matched by, and inextricably linked to, those companies’ skyrocketing spending on chips, data centers, and other AI infrastructure. The AI data center boom already represents the largest private sector capital investment project in history, with spending on AI infra-structure in 2026 accounting for a larger share of GDP than “the Manhattan Project, the expansion of electricity, the Apollo space program, building the interstate highway system, broadband buildout during the dot-com bubble, and every other capital effort in U.S. history, except for the Louisiana Purchase and maybe the peak of railroad construction.” 34 But AI capital expenditures far exceed, and have been growing much more quickly than, revenues from AI products and services, and AI companies are borrowing heavily to make up the difference.

c. Trillions of dollars in debt, with more coming every day 

How is the AI industry paying for roughly a trillion dollars per year in infrastructure while bringing in only a fraction of that amount in sales? At first, the AI spending boom was financed primarily through the non-AI cash flows of Big Tech giants, with venture capital and private equity investments providing an additional boost. This generated little economic concern because it was principally the tech giants’ own money at risk. But as the costs of the AI infra-structure boom continued to balloon, the companies at its center started ramping up their borrowing in mid-2025, leading to an explosion in AI-linked debt over the past year. With the hyperscalers’ cash flows turning negative as of the summer of 2026, debt will be the lynchpin for AI infrastructure financing going forward — and its greatest source of risk. In their most recent earnings statements, the nine biggest hyperscalers and chipmakers (Alphabet, Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, Oracle, and SpaceX) reported a total of $595 billion in long-term debt on their balance sheets. But far more debt lurks off the companies’ balance sheets. In August, the Wall Street Journal calculat-ed that the total off-balance-sheet commitments of those 21 

companies totaled at least $3.1 trillion. 50 (By comparison, the total size of the subprime mortgage market was $1.5 trillion, or $2.3 trillion in today’s dollars, at its 2007 peak, as shown in Figure 7. 51 )Much of that off-balance-sheet debt underpins loans taken out by other companies involved in the data center construction boom. Bloomberg describes such AI-linked borrowing as “all-consuming” for credit markets, with AI companies turning to every corner of debt markets, from traditional corporate bonds to project finance to more exotic forms of debt, to finance their spending. 52 The riskiest debts in the AI ecosystem may be those tied to the neoclouds , the term of art for companies like CoreWeave and Nebius that focus on developing data centers and leasing access to the GPUs they contain to generative AI model developers. Unable to obtain the investment-grade financing that the tech giants can ac-cess, neoclouds must pay steep interest rates, sometimes reaching well into the double digits. 53 To obtain additional financing, neoclouds are increasingly putting up AI chips as collateral. 54 But stagnating AI demand would both threaten the income streams that neoclouds are count-ing on to meet their loan obligations and drive down the value of the collateral — a combination that could create toxic debt in the wake of an AI downturn. 55 As described further below, the AI ecosystem’s interconnectedness means that both tech giants and financial institutions have significant exposure to the debt that these weaker players in the AI industry are fast accumulating. 

3. Funny accounting, incestuous financial arrangements, hidden debt, and other chicanery 

Why would investors keep pouring money into a technology that is racking up huge amounts of debt while bringing in revenues that are only a fraction of its costs? Persistent hype surrounding AI is a key part of the answer; bubbles are irrational by nature, and the narratives that inflate them are often impervious to conflicting evidence while the bubble is intact. But another key feature of bubbles is that they often are inflated and sustained by dubious financial tactics that paint a deceptively rosy picture of the overvalued sector or asset class. That very much appears to be the case with generative AI. 

a. Revenue games and circular financing 

The leading generative AI model developers, Anthropic and OpenAI, are currently privately held. b. Hidden liabilities: Depreciation trickery and off-balance-sheet debt 

AI companies are also using highly dubious accounting techniques and opaque data center financing arrange-ments to obscure the full extent of their liabilities, partic-ularly when it comes to their capital expenditures on chips and data center construction. Hyperscalers are taking advantage of an accounting loophole that allows them to dramatically understate their expenses by claiming that their AI chips will last for five to six years even though their useful economic life appears to be significantly shorter, a tactic known as understating 

depreciation .73 The rapid churn cycle of AI chips is a func-tion both of the speed with which more advanced chips are developed and released, with Nvidia now releasing new chips every year, as well as the fact that GPUs can wear out in three years or less with heavy use. 74 Hyperscalers could be forced to collectively write down or write off tens or even hundreds of billions of dollars if their chips die or are retired significantly earlier than they are claiming on their balance sheets. 75 AI companies are using other accounting tricks to keep the bulk of their AI obligations off their balance sheets altogether. Hyperscalers are increasingly parking debt tied to data center construction projects in shell companies called special-purpose vehicles (SPVs). For example, Meta and private credit giant Blue Owl Capital, partnering with investment fund giant PIMCO, set up an SPV that took out a $26 billion loan to begin construction on a massive data center complex in Louisiana. 76 Even though Meta is the data center’s sole tenant 77 and has backstopped the debt on the shell company’s behalf, 78 the arrangement does not appear as debt on Meta’s balance sheet because, technically, it is the shell company that is taking out the loan. B. RELATED ECONOMIC TROUBLE SPOTS 

Given the scale of the AI bubble and the alarmingly fast-growing mass of debt attached to it, the economy could be headed for trouble even if the bubble were the only potential source of economic risk. Unfortunately, the economy has other trouble spots that are connected with, adjacent to, or potentially correlated with the AI bubble and that could accelerate and deepen an AI crash. The sprawling private credit ecosystem far predates the AI bubble but has become deeply intertwined with it (Sub-section 1). Cryptocurrencies are speculative investments that tend to fall in value when tech stocks do (Subsection 2). The AI bubble itself has spawned new economic weak points that could worsen the fallout from an AI crash (Subsection 3).

This includes private equity firms, which have made lending through affiliated private credit funds an increasingly prominent part of their operations. Because many of the largest firms that purchase private owner-ship shares in companies (private equity) also engage in non-bank lending (private credit), we will use the umbrella term private investment firms to refer to the financial firms that focus on managing private capital funds.

An AI crash would deal the private credit sector another major blow. Along with corporate bonds, private credit has been a leading source of debt financing for data center con-struction, AI chip purchases, and related AI infrastructure investments. Morgan Stanley projected that private credit funds could hold as much as $800 billion worth of data center debt by 2028. 100 Given the stress that private credit funds are already experiencing, it is unclear whether or how they could withstand an AI reversal. As discussed further below, the danger extends beyond the private credit funds that made the loans. Private credit is also deeply interconnected with banks and life insur-ers. Banks finance private credit funds and their portfolio companies, while life insurers invest policyholder premiums in private credit funds and the loans they make. Banks, insurers, and private credit funds can therefore be exposed to the same borrowers and assets. If AI-linked loans default or lose value, losses could spread through these channels and expose several sectors within the financial system to heightened risk at once. 

2. Crypto 

There is evidence that cryptocurrencies tend to fall when tech stocks fall, 101 and the failure of a series of cryptocur-rency-linked banks in 2023 demonstrated that crypto shocks can become a source of contagion in the financial system. The bursting of a crypto bubble and the subsequent collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX and other crypto-currency firms contributed to three of the ten largest bank failures in U.S. history in 2023. The ensuing crypto winter erased $2 trillion in crypto value, with millions of investors wiped out. 102 Federal regulators backstopped the failed banks, which were deeply enmeshed with the crypto indus-try, including bailing out tech companies, wealthy investors, and executives who held deposits in those banks above the insured deposit limit. 103 Stablecoins — a type of digital currency that has its price pegged to a specific value, typically the U.S. dollar — pres-ents yet another source of financial risk. Most stablecoins are backed by highly liquid and stable assets like cash reserves or government securities that help to stabilize and maintain the asset’s price. However, a 2023 Bank of International Settlements study found that not a single one of 68 stablecoins — including all major stablecoins — had been able to maintain their peg parity at all times, a fact that became especially apparent during the 2022-2023 crypto market turmoil. 104 A Federal Reserve Bank of New York study found that redemptions “accelerate signifi-cantly” when stablecoin values dip below $1. 105 J.P. Morgan Research noted that “the effects of a massive [stablecoin] liquidation could spill over to other markets, destabilizing the traditional banking system.” 106 The current administration’s efforts to expand the crypto industry, insert it into mainstream financial products like workers’ 401(k) retirement savings, and entwine stablecoins more deeply with the banking system are increasing these risks. 

3. AI-driven brittleness 

The AI boom itself is also creating new economic trouble spots, which could make the economy less able to absorb the shocks that would follow the bursting of the bubble. Most of these new pain points are outgrowths of the data center boom, which has cannibalized essential resources from other parts of the economy. Data centers’ insatiable energy appetite is straining con-sumers’ pocketbooks and creating new risks for utilities and other companies tied to the electric grid. 107 Utilities and grid operators have issued tens of billions of dollars in bonds and contracted for hundreds of gigawatts’ worth of new infrastructure to meet anticipated data center demand. 108 Those entities would face a crisis of their own if a substantial portion of that anticipated demand evaporated due to an AI crash, potentially leading utilities to either significantly increase rates on households and small businesses or risk defaulting on their debt. 28 

AI is straining supplies of other crucial resources as well. Many data centers use enormous quantities of water for cooling. Unlike with electricity, it is often not even possi-ble to scale up water supplies in regions near data centers, most of which are being built in areas where water supplies are already stretched, like the arid Southwestern U.S. 109 The data center boom is also leading to scarcity in supplies of key resources such as construction materials and semi-conductors. 110 As the Wall Street Journal warned in June 2026, the AI buildout is “beginning to push up prices on everything from smartphones to electricity,” fueling a “third wave of inflation.” 111 The sheer scale of the financial and material resources involved means that the AI boom may be creating other economic soft spots that will be difficult to detect or measure until after the bubble bursts. Economic shocks often expose weaknesses in the economy that were not readily apparent beforehand. We won’t know the full extent of economic activity that would come under threat in the event of an AI crash unless and until such a crash occurs. 29 

# How an AI crash could start and spread PART TWO 30 

# Part II: How an AI crash could start and spread 

Having outlined the AI bubble’s key characteristics and risks, we now turn to the question of why and how the bubble might burst as well as how the effects of an AI crash might ripple (or rip) through the rest of the economy. By “crash,” we do not necessarily mean that any specif-ic company or companies will go bankrupt, although, as we explain, major firm failures are certainly a possibility. Rather, a crash occurs when the value of a particular class of assets — here, shares in AI companies as well as debt linked to those companies and to the chips and data centers they own, lease, and operate — falls precipitous-ly. 112 While some crashes are dramatic and triggered by a specific event (such as the collapse of Lehman Brothers in 2008), they can also play out gradually over weeks or months as the market loses confidence in the industry (like the bursting of the dot-com bubble in 2000). In either event, they typically are due to risks that accumu-lated months or years before the crash. Regardless of the particular form it might take, the AI sector’s dominance in both equity and credit markets means that an AI crash would likely be felt well beyond the AI industry. While not intended to be a prediction of a specific sequence of events, Parts II and III are organized in a manner that allows us to describe how key sources of risk, contagion effects, and other aspects of a potential AI crash relate to each other. In brief outline: several forces are increasing the odds of a crash, which would likely start with weaker AI players; those players are deeply intercon-nected with the Big Tech companies; the Big Tech com-panies play a central role in the broader stock market, and AI-linked debt similarly dominates credit markets; and an AI-centered market crash thus could have severe effects on financial markets and the real economy. 113 Part II will focus on why the likelihood of an AI crash is increasing and how the bursting of the AI bubble could devastate the tech sector. It proceeds as follows: • AI companies will likely struggle to earn the returns necessary to meet their obligations due to a combination of forces that tend to increase the AI industry’s costs and constrain its revenue growth (Section A). • The most probable starting points for an AI sector crash are the most precarious AI model developers (OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX), the fragile data center debt associated with the overstretched neoclouds, and the shaky hyperscaler Oracle (Section B). • Regardless of where an AI crash might originate, the interconnectedness of the AI ecosystem means that a collapse would threaten to drag down the rest of the tech sector, including some of the largest tech companies (Section C). 

A. WHY AI COMPANIES COULD STRUGGLE TO PAY THEIR MOUNTING BILLS 

Thus far, AI companies have been able to cover the massive gap between their revenues and their spending by raising unprecedented amounts of money from investors in the form of both equity and debt. But one can only go on so long raising money from Peter to pay Paul (just ask Charles Ponzi and Bernie Madoff). Sooner or later, companies must be able to pay their bills from (actual, non-circular) revenues. Just as important, sustaining the infrastructure and stock market booms requires that financial market participants maintain their confidence in generative AI’s path to profitability. As John Maynard Keynes observed, market sentiment is often driven less by rational assessment of financial prospects than by “animal spirits,” and “if animal spirits are dimmed and spontaneous optimism falters, leaving us to depend on nothing but a mathematical expectation, enterprise will fade and die.” 114 If it becomes apparent that tech companies will be unable to cover their costs or that lenders have lost confidence in their ability to do so, market optimism could turn quickly into pessimism, precipitating a crash. With AI-related capital expenditures continuing to in-crease and large swaths of data center construction loans coming due over the next two to three years, markets will be watching the AI industry’s financial trajectory closely. This section describes the imposing and possibly insur-mountable obstacles that could prevent AI companies from increasing their collective revenues quickly enough to pay their bills and satisfy investors’ expectations. The forces described in this section (see figure) tend to drive down revenues or increase costs, are already visible, interact with and reinforce each other, and seem poised to continue, if not worsen, over time. 31 

This section focuses on forces that are, in the main, endogenous or particular to the AI industry. Additional forces, particularly rising interest rates, are pressuring borrowers across the economy and could eventually squeeze companies on shakier financial footing into de-fault, particularly those (like many tied to the data center boom) that will need to refinance in order to pay existing debts. Shortly before this paper went to press, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 and signaled that further rate hikes were likely. 115 Such monetary tightening notably preceded the bursting of many speculative bubbles, including the dot-com bub-ble. 116 

1. There may not be trillions of dollars’ worth of generative AI demand 

It is an open question whether demand for genera-tive-AI-based products and services will be strong enough or come fast enough to spur the revenue growth needed to justify AI industry spending. The additional demand required is unprecedented — no emerging technology has ever had a break-even point in the trillions of dollars per year in revenue. Whether sufficient demand emerges will depend on whether businesses (and, to a lesser degree, consumers) start seeing stronger returns on their invest-ments in AI products and services and how quickly those returns materialize. The guiding assumption of the AI boom is that genera-tive AI will massively increase productivity, particularly by automating tasks typically performed by white-collar workers. So far, however, there is scant evidence that generative AI is driving significant productivity increases, much less transformational ones. 117 At the macroeconomic level, AI had no obvious impact on productivity in 2025 118 nor in the first half of 2026. 119 Zoom in to the level of individual businesses, and the picture is much the same. 

Multiple studies, including from organizations otherwise notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest generative AI is not accelerating productivity or otherwise generating positive returns on investment for most businesses. 120 This may partly explain why the number of U.S. adults who said they were using AI at work declined noticeably between mid-2025 (46%) and mid-2026 (33%). 121 

Even if dramatic productivity gains from AI do emerge at some point, their arrival may not come quickly enough to cover the industry’s fast-mounting bills. Returns on tech-

Railroads and the internet were transformational technologies, but the speculative bubbles they generated burst because it took far longer than investors expected for businesses to reorganize their operations in ways that unlocked the technologies’ commercial potential. To that point, a recent study by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis found that while corporate executives frequently mention AI-driven productivity increases on earnings calls, 95% of those mentions are about expected future gains rather than gains that have already appeared. 122 Some companies that attempted to replace their human workers with generative AI have actually had to reverse course because the technology simply was not up to the task. 123 For example, the Buy Now, Pay Later firm Klarna attempted to replace customer service representatives with chatbots en masse, only to discover that, “[w] hile AI may be efficient, it turns out it’s not great at handling nuance, empathy, or angry customers yelling about missed payments.” 124 The company ended up quietly hiring back hundreds of laid off workers and was considering hiring gig workers to fill the remaining roles. 125 

2. Fierce competition is pushing down the industry’s margins 

Even if demand for generative AI picks up, the AI indus-try’s frenzied competition will put downward pressure on AI revenues. Because none of the core technologies underpinning generative AI enjoy intellectual property protection, no company has an effective “moat” to keep competitors out. This has resulted in a crowded ecosys-tem where numerous well-capitalized corporations offer models that are comparable enough in their quality and capabilities that many customers switch between them based mainly on price differences, 126 a process called 

commoditization .AI companies have proven that they can quickly offer competing products whenever a rival identifies a produc-tive application of generative AI. Indeed, the firms pile in whenever a use case shows even a hint of commercial potential. Thus, when Anthropic successfully launched Claude Code in March 2025, it was followed just three months later by OpenAI’s Codex and Google’s Gemini Code Assist, 127 and it took mere hours for OpenAI to strike a deal with the Pentagon after the Trump adminis-tration banned the use of Anthropic’s models. 128 This summer, the industry began to descend into a brutal form of market competition: a price war. In early June, reporting indicated that Anthropic and OpenAI were considering drastic price cuts in an effort to win customers ahead of their anticipated IPOs. By July, Silicon Valley model developers were attempting to outdo each other by offering steep discounts of up to 75% for access to their models. 129 With Alphabet (Gemini), Amazon (Nova Act), Microsoft (Copilot), Meta (Llama and now Muse), SpaceX/xAI (Grok), and even Nvidia (Nemotron) offering their own models, Silicon Valley’s AI behemoths are likely to continue to struggle to raise prices without losing customers to rivals. Competition from Chinese model developers is putting further downward pressure on prices. In contrast to the mainly proprietary models of Silicon Valley model developers, most Chinese generative AI companies offer models on an open-weights basis, which allows businesses and individuals to access, modify, and build on models without paying a license fee. Open-weights models are particularly attractive for companies building their own AI tools, including the startups and large businesses that currently account for most commercial use of generative AI. 130 Chinese models have been rapidly gaining ground on their Silicon Valley rivals among commercial users. 131 

3. Generative AI is expensive at every point in its lifecycle 

While demand and competition challenges make it diffi-cult for model developers to raise prices, the technology’s very high costs mean that they will not be able to keep prices low for long either. In addition to enormous upfront capital expenditures on chips, data centers, and support-ing infrastructure, generative AI requires hefty costs throughout models’ lifecycle. Model training requires electricity to power AI chips and additional energy and/ or water to cool them. More sophisticated models require more computational power to train and thus more energy and water to power and cool the specialized chips. As a result, the costs of Anthropic and OpenAI’s new frontier models have been increasing by orders of magnitude with each new generation, even as AI chips have become more efficient. 132 Each new generative AI model thus comes to market with a large bill already attached to it. The costs continue to mount when customers access generative AI models. Each time someone asks a chat-bot to answer a question or create an image, additional computational power, energy, and cooling are needed to process the query and generate a response, a process called inference . While the latest chips are more efficient at processing tokens , the technical term for the fragments of text and other data that generative AI models process and generate, more sophisticated “reasoning” and espe-33 

cially “agentic” models consume far more tokens when responding to queries, which can cause overall inference costs to rise even as the per-token cost falls. 133 The cost of key inputs is also increasing due to the memory chip shortage and other supply chain constraints, further increasing operational expenses. 134 

4. Resource constraints and infrastructure bottlenecks 

In addition to internal price and cost challenges, there are numerous external factors that could delay or drive up the cost of the data centers and other infrastructure needed to train and run AI models or even stop projects from be-ing completed at all. A fierce and still-rising backlash to AI in general and data centers in particular across the politi-cal spectrum has developed over the past year, 135 including in regions of the U.S. that are considered tech-friendly and/or pro-business. 136 Community opposition to data centers has scuttled a number of data center projects and delayed many others. 137 For projects that do get off the ground, supply chain challenges are leading to delays and higher prices on key inputs such as construction materials, power generation, and memory chips. 138 Utilities are also struggling to bring enough new power generation capacity online to meet data centers’ enormous power needs, forc-ing many data center developers to install gas-powered power generators on-site. 139 Navigating the logistics of data center construction is proving to be exceptionally challenging for many of the companies that have taken on these huge infrastructure projects. Several hyperscale data center projects have been canceled, 140 and only half of AI computing capac-ity scheduled to come online over the next two years is expected to do so by its target date. 141 These delays and cancelations will limit the computational capacity AI com-panies are counting on to generate the revenue that they will desperately need to cover their costs and convince lenders to continue extending credit to them. 

5. The squeeze 

The industry’s brutal economics are not likely to improve anytime soon. Even if demand for generative AI were to pick up significantly, competition — both among the big U.S. companies and with their open-weights Chinese rivals — will continue to be intense. Those forces will apply unrelenting downward pressure on prices even as high costs and resource constraints squeeze companies from the opposite direction. These factors are a dangerous mix for an industry that has accumulated trillions of dollars in on- and off-balance-sheet debt, a vast and immovable cost. With those costs continuing to accumulate far faster than revenues from generative AI products and services, a financial reckoning for the industry appears increasingly likely. 

B. POINTS OF FRAGILITY IN THE AI ECOSYSTEM 

It is impossible to tell when a speculative bubble will end, much less what might burst or deflate it or which com-panies will be the first to fall. That said, the generative AI ecosystem has a few particularly glaring points of fragility: · Three model developers , namely Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX, which have made ambitious financial commitments but are earning only a fraction of the revenues necessary to meet them (Subsection 1); · Neocloud-linked data center debt , which is often financed through a brittle stack of leases and loans, the timely repayment of which depends on numerous factors beyond any one party’s control (Subsection 2); and · Oracle , a hyperscaler that has taken on more than $120 billion in long-term debt and $260 billion in off-balance sheet lease commitments in a gambit to become a dominant AI cloud provider (Subsection 3). 

1. Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX: The fragile model developers 

While all model developers face the pressures described in Section A, the biggest hyperscalers — namely Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft — enjoy a considerable cushion thanks to the enormous profits they earn from their non-AI operations. Anthropic and OpenAI do not have that luxury. They are effectively “pure-play” AI companies whose continued existence depends on the commercial success of their generative AI products and services. They thus are at a high risk of insolvency if gen-erative AI sales growth slows or investors lose confidence in the industry’s steep path to profitability. Anthropic and OpenAI’s hundreds of billions of dollars in future data center lease and chip purchase commitments give them little margin for error when it comes to meeting their extremely ambitious revenue growth projections. SpaceX, unlike OpenAI and Anthropic, has notable non-AI revenue streams. But SpaceX is scarcely less vulnerable. Musk’s company has deeply negative profit margins and a significant amount of long-term debt, including $25 billion 34 

in bonds that the company issued shortly after its IPO. 142 The value of those bonds soon fell sharply, suggesting that investors doubt SpaceX’s ultimate ability to repay them. 143 SpaceX is also more of a generative AI pure-play than its name and reputation suggest. Its annual revenues, cur-rently $19 billion, are a tiny fraction of the legacy tech giants’, which range from $214 billion (Meta) to $743 billion (Amazon). Moreover, while SpaceX’s current rev-enues come mostly from its rocket and satellite internet divisions, the company’s prospectus makes clear that its future business plans center on generative AI, particularly building “orbital AI compute” — that is, data centers in space — and the company spent $40 billion to purchase the AI coding startup Cursor. 144 SpaceX’s massive in-vestments in AI mean that its future business, like those of Anthropic, OpenAI, and the neoclouds, depends on generative AI going from deeply unprofitable to wildly profitable within a few years. The shaky financial position of Anthropic, OpenAI, and SpaceX leaves them especially vulnerable to the forces outlined in Section A. Model developers’ biggest costs, namely purchases and leases of chips and data centers, are set years in advance through multi-year contracts. Any departure of cost-conscious customers would force model developers to try to squeeze an even larger profit margin out of each remaining customer to cover those effectively fixed costs. To do so, they may have to raise prices even more, which could cause still more customers to flee, forcing further price increases in a negative feedback loop. A desire to avoid such a trap helps explain why model de-velopers offered access to their models at a deep discount to their actual cost for several years, which for a long while meant that AI companies lost money on virtually all their users, 145 including those with premium subscrip-tions. 146 That is not a sustainable business model. An-thropic appeared to bow to that reality when it switched from subscriptions to usage-based pricing for enterprise customers earlier this year. 147 While this was not billed as a price increase, that is exactly what it was. The move apparently succeeded in raising Anthropic’s revenues for the quarter, but what unfolded thereafter was telling. Many customers, having gotten used to the industry’s previous buffet-style pricing, got sticker shock when they had to pay a la carte . One company report-edly ran up a $500 million bill to Anthropic in just three months. 148 Unsurprisingly, several companies began to question whether it was worth paying the new, higher prices for access to leading AI models. Some Anthropic customers, including Microsoft and the crypto exchange Coinbase, quietly switched to in-house or open-weights models to cut costs. 149 Others, including Uber and Walmart, chose to cap their AI usage rather than pay more for it. 150 Weeks later, Anthropic and OpenAI re-versed course, triggering the industry’s burgeoning price war. Enterprise customers have gone from racking up huge, unexpected AI bills to receiving millions in free AI tokens. 151 

Moreover, while Anthropic and OpenAI continue to sign chip and cloud contracts that commit them to train and run ever-more powerful and expensive models, there are growing signs that most businesses are not interested in 

paying for more powerful and expensive models. 

Anthropic’s most recent commercially available frontier model, Fable, received a tepid commercial reception; two months after its release, the model had plateaued at about 11% of businesses’ Anthropic token spending, with only 6% of its customers choosing to upgrade from the developer’s older models. 152 The lack of transparency into generative AI’s baseline costs and true revenues makes it difficult to determine how financially sustainable model developers’ operations are. But the events following the spring 2026 price in-creases suggest that they are struggling to find a sustain-able path to profitability. Harsh choices thus may await the model developers: keep prices low and hemorrhage money, or raise them and watch customers flee, be it to cheaper models, to deeper-pocketed rivals who can better absorb losses, or to human workers. 

2. Neoclouds and brittle data center debt 

Vulnerable as the model developers are, the neoclouds and their data center development projects, both of which are showing signs of serious financial strain, could also become an origin point for a crisis. Most neoclouds’ bonds are rated as junk and carry correspondingly high interest rates. 153 External pressures are hitting their data-cen-ter development efforts hard; rising energy costs, other resource constraints, and growing community opposition to data centers are delaying or outright blocking many projects. 154 So far, the neoclouds have mostly been able to pay their bills thanks to circular financing arrangements, leases, and other deals with other generative AI ecosystem partic-ipants — particularly Nvidia, whose chips fill their data centers. But those data centers are being financed by ex-ceptionally brittle debt, often involving consecutive loans that could easily go into default if there are construction 35 

delays, cost overruns, or model developers who break or choose not to renew leases. 155 The construction of major data centers often involves numerous entities, each of which has billions of dollars riding on every other entity fulfilling their responsibilities. For example, OpenAI is using the Nvidia chips at a huge data center in Abilene, Texas to train and run new generative AI models. But OpenAI does not own the data center or the chips. Rather, it is effectively leasing both from Oracle using money OpenAI has raised from its investors, including Softbank and Nvidia. It only gets more complicated from there, because Oracle does not own the Abilene facility either. Oracle leases it from a neocloud, Crusoe Energy, but (wait for it) Crusoe doesn’t fully own it either. Rather, it is co-developing the site with private investment firm Blue Owl Capital and an investment fund called Primary Digital Infrastructure (PDI). Together, the trio financed the site’s development using $5 billion in cash and a $10 billion loan from JPMC taken out by a shell company sponsored by Crusoe, Blue Owl, and PDI. 156 Yet another entity, Lancium, owns the land on which the data center is being developed. Such multilayered structures are precarious. If the model developer is unable to fulfill the terms of the lease or the neocloud cannot complete the construction of the data cen-ter, each of the other parties involved in the project would face billions in potential losses unless another entity can be roped in to fulfill the obligations of the delinquent party. If generative AI demand continues to rise and the other actors in this stack have the financing required to meet their demands, that is doable; indeed, when OpenAI pulled out of a planned extension of the Abilene complex, Microsoft leased it instead. 157 But if there is a wave of broken leases, as would likely occur after a broad stagnation in generative AI demand, replacement tenants would be hard to come by and huge amounts of data center debt could become toxic. 3. Oracle’s all-or-nothing bet on rapid AI transformation 

As the above description of the neoclouds’ financial hur-dles suggests, the finances of many companies in the AI ecosystem depend on the ability of OpenAI and Anthrop-ic to pay their bills. Perhaps no company is more reliant on and exposed to the pure-play model developers, however, than deeply indebted Oracle. Oracle’s capital expenditures rival those of Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and Meta, but its revenues are only roughly 30% of Meta’s, the smallest of Oracle’s hyper-scaler rivals. Consequently, Oracle has been forced to borrow heavily, racking up roughly $120 billion in long-term debt, 160 including $43 billion added in the past year, 161 on top of $260 billion in off-balance-sheet debt, mostly in the form of lease commitments. 162 Much of this debt is fueling a spending spree on chips and data center capacity that Oracle plans to sell or lease to OpenAI, which has committed to spend $300 billion to access Oracle’s infrastructure. 163 If OpenAI fails to grow its revenues fast enough and breaks a substantial number of its commitments, Larry El-lison’s company would be hit especially hard. Markets al-ready seem to think that Oracle’s prospects have become shaky, with its credit ratings hovering just above junk and investors having to pay high premiums for Oracle’s credit default swaps (essentially, insurance that is paid out if Oracle defaults on its debt). 164 It would not take a full-on collapse of OpenAI to threaten Oracle’s viability, as Oracle itself came close to admitting in its most recent annual financial report. The report acknowl-edged that the corporation’s debt pile means that it faces a risk of being “locked into multi-year commitments for ex-cess data center space and related capital expenditures, as well as associated financings, without receiving correspond-ing revenue” if Oracle “overestimate[s] customer demand or any of [its] key customers are unable to pay.” 165 Moreover, and similar to many neoclouds, Oracle faces risk from the mismatched time horizons of its long-term debt and model developers’ shorter-term leases. In a gen-erative AI downturn, as Oracle’s financial report states, “if customers do not renew their contracts, [Oracle] may be unable to re-lease, repurpose or assign” its data center capacity “on acceptable terms, if at all.” 166 Oracle is also exposed to data center construction delays and “cost increases related to design, engineering, permitting, con-struction, utility interconnection, equipment delivery and contractor performance.” 167 While Oracle frames these challenges merely as threats to its “profitability,” the high cost of insuring against an Oracle default suggests that markets fear they could leave the industry stalwart unable to pay its debts. 168 

C. BIG TECH’S DEEP EXPOSURE TO AN AI CRASH 

How, and how much, an AI crash affects the tech giants depends on its nature and depth. If a crash is shallow or short-lived, the failure of smaller AI industry players might be a potential boon for the tech giants; Amazon, Google, and Microsoft would be eager to use the collapse of Oracle or the neoclouds to cement their cloud domi-nance, and any Big Tech behemoth would love to snap up OpenAI and Anthropic’s AI products and market share on the cheap. Such a series of events would mirror the outcome of the 2008 financial crisis, which ended with the biggest banks becoming still bigger, and the dot-com bubble, which not only spared but ultimately strengthened Amazon, Apple, 37 

Google, and Microsoft as many of their potential rivals withered or died. If generative AI demand merely fails to meet loftiest expectations or takes slightly longer than expected to fulfill them, we could see a similar wave of consolidation where the surviving giants carve up the AI market between them. 169 (Though, as we note in Part IV, the federal government should block any such mergers and rein in anticompetitive practices across the industry). But the tech giants may be more vulnerable than they seem. Despite their dominance, Nvidia and the hyperscal-ers’ extensive web of connections with the rest of the AI ecosystem means that they would be deeply and directly affected by a severe crash originating with the ecosys-tem’s smaller and weaker players (Subsection 1). Moreover, Big Tech companies have placed their own massive bets on generative AI, as illustrated by their stakes in model developers and the trillions of dollars in on- and off-balance-sheet debt they have assumed to build data centers and purchase chips and compute capacity. The collapse of a major model developer or a series of failed data center projects would likely create a major shock affecting all those invest-ments. Nvidia, which dominates the chip market, is deeply exposed to such a shock because of its massive forward purchase commitments and circular financing arrangements with model developers and neoclouds (Subsection 2). Simi-larly, the hyperscalers’ huge pile of debt, much of it off-bal-ance-sheet, and circular-financing-driven-revenues mean that they are far more exposed to stagnation in generative AI demand than their enormous profits suggest (Subsection 3). 

1. Contagion within the AI ecosystem 

As previously noted, the various players in the AI ecosys-tem are deeply interconnected with each other. Most of the Magnificent Seven’s earnings growth in the second quarter of 2026 came not from increasing sales, but from the increasing value of their investments in other AI com-panies. 170 Nvidia and the hyperscalers have also directly guaranteed hundreds of billions of dollars in loans and lease payments by neoclouds and model developers. Nvid-ia alone is exposed to $297 billion in off-balance-sheet debt through its backstop guarantees and purchase com-mitments to other AI companies, leading The Economist to dub Nvidia “the central bank of AI.” 171 But these liabilities do not appear on Nvidia’s balance sheet. 172 Similarly, Alphabet has guaranteed $44 billion of Anthropic’s leases but has marked the value of that potential liability at just $815 million on its balance sheet. 173 The extensive web of equity stakes, cloud computing contracts, lease and purchase agreements, financing ar-rangements, and debt guarantees connecting chipmakers, hyperscalers, model developers, and neoclouds mean that a crash in any one corner of the AI ecosystem would likely spread to others. 

2. Nvidia is deeply exposed to acute stress within the AI ecosystem 

Nvidia is the most valuable company in history, but the company has hundreds of billions of dollars tied up in financing arrangements involving OpenAI, Anthropic, and the neoclouds. Those deals illustrate the degree to which the chip giant is counting on those companies as a source of future demand for its chips. The greatest threat to Nvidia would arise if the demand for its chips experienced a reversal, which have historically been common in the chip industry. 174 The lengthy lead time, often a year or more, 175 between when a customer orders an Nvidia chip and when the chip is activated in a data center means that there is an enormous amount of GPU capacity moving through the manufacturing, pack-aging, 176 server integration, and data center construction pipeline at any given time. A stagnation or decline in gen-erative AI demand, particularly if it leads to the collapse of Oracle, a major model developer, or a significant number of neoclouds, would create a volatile mix of demand and supply shocks in the AI chip market. Nvidia’s customers could default on or cancel orders, reducing future de-mand, while GPUs already installed in data centers might be offered for rental or sale at distressed prices. Such a glut in GPU capacity would severely weaken the market for Nvidia’s chips. Nvidia’s business model has left it increasingly vulnerable to such market shocks. Nvidia has a substantial stockpile of cash ($63 billion as of July 2026), but the company dis-closed $511 billion worth of forward purchase commitments and debt guarantees on its Q2 2026 earnings statement 177 — and that does not include the additional guarantees Nvidia will provide under another 12-digit financing ar-rangement the company announced the following month. 178 If the demand for its AI chips were to plunge, Nvidia’s cash flows would dry up, but those obligations would remain. In such a scenario, Nvidia could burn through its cash quickly. 

3. The hyperscalers’ hidden vulnerability 

The hyperscalers’ profitability seems as unassailable as Nvidia’s, with Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft each boasting annual profits that approach or exceed $100 billion. But, like Nvidia, the hyperscalers are deeply vulnerable to an AI crash. 38 

The hyperscalers’ financial statements are already showing signs of strain. Over the past two years, the hyperscalers have gone from financing AI infrastructure spending from operating cash flows to issuing massive amounts of debt (and, more recently, equity) to cover their capital expenditures. 179 Much like Nvidia, while the tech giants’ market domi-nance has allowed them to accumulate a massive cash pile (a combined $533 billion as of the end of Q2 2026), their even larger debt obligations and breakneck spending have left them in a precarious position. This summer, Alphabet reported negative free cash flow for the first time in its two-plus decades as a publicly traded company. 180 Am-azon likewise turned cash-flow negative earlier this year, and Meta and Microsoft are on the cusp of doing so. 181 By early 2027, the top four hyperscalers’ combined free cash flow is expected to turn negative as their capital expendi-tures continue to increase (see figure). 182 Much of the hyperscalers’ skyrocketing obligations are accumulating off their balance sheets in the form of future lease and purchase commitments. In their Q2 2026 earnings statements, Alphabet ($896 billion), 183 Amazon ($267 billion), 184 Meta ($696 billion), 185 and Microsoft ($523 billion) 186 each reported future lease and purchase commitments far exceeding the annual revenues of nearly all (or all, in Alphabet’s case) Fortune 500 companies. 

Add those nearly $2.4 trillion in off-balance-sheet commitments to the companies’ $342 billion in bal-ance-sheet debt, and the total obligations of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft as of September 2026 stood at roughly $2.7 trillion. That is one and a half times their combined annual revenues and five times their combined annual profits — revenues and profits that, again, appear to be artificially inflated by dubious financial arrangements and accounting methods. 

If demand growth for generative AI services were merely to slow significantly, narrowing the technology’s path to profitability, the hyperscalers could be forced to cancel the construction of many of the data centers that they are rushing to build. If generative AI demand actually fell, the giants would likely have to mothball some existing data centers as well. It is here that the hyperscalers’ extensive use of shell com-panies and off-balance-sheet debt would face its toughest test. By structuring their future data center obligations as lease agreements with shell companies, the hyperscalers apparently hope that they will be able to walk away more easily if the generative AI market reverses (or, at least, they want to convince auditors and markets that they will be able to do so). # Why an AI crash would pose serious macroeconomic risks PART THREE 41 

# Part III: Why an AI crash would pose serious macroeconomic risks 

The bursting of speculative bubbles and resulting market downturns can spark broader economic crises, but they do not necessarily do so. If a crash stays largely contained within a single sector (as with the dot-com bubble) or the shock dissipates almost as quickly as it materialized (as with Black Monday in 1987), the economy may experi-ence short-term pain but often will bounce back quickly. Unfortunately, the AI bubble’s unprecedented size and AI companies’ interconnectedness with the broader economy and financial system would make an AI crash exceedingly difficult to contain. As financial journalist John Cassidy has explained, there are three main ways in which a stock market crash or other collapse in asset prices can damage the economy. 199 First, “it can damage the banking system, especially if banks have lent a lot of money against assets whose value has collapsed.” 200 This was the primary force in the 2008 financial crisis. Second, “[i]t can reduce consumer spend-ing by making people poorer.” 201 This and closely related forces were key mechanisms through which the 1929 crash led to the Great Depression. 202 Finally, “it can hit investment spending because firms find it more difficult to raise money.” 203 This force, which played out to partic-ularly damaging effect in the aftermath of the Panic of 1873 and during Japan’s “Lost Decade” of the 1990s, is even more severe if the crash involves a significant quan-tity of toxic debt or otherwise creates stranded assets, which act as a chronic drag on economic growth. An AI crash would threaten heavy doses of all three types of economic damage. Big Tech’s dominance of major indi-ces means that turmoil in the AI sector would threaten a broader stock market crash, particularly given the growing amount of leverage in the stock market and the large share of stocks held through passive index funds (Section A). The deep, and still deepening, exposure of private credit firms and life insurers to AI-linked debt provide fast-growing pathways for an AI crash to spill over into the banking system, in addition to banks’ growing direct exposure to AI risk (Section B). The size of the AI bubble means that a collapse in AI-connected asset prices would threaten downward spirals in the real economy (Section C). The effect on investment could be just as catastrophic, particularly if the crash leaves behind a significant amount of stranded chips and data centers (Section D). The accu-mulation of these factors has created a veritable minefield of economic hazards that markets and policymakers alike would struggle to navigate in the wake of an AI crash (Section E). 

A. LEVERAGE, PASSIVE INVESTING, AND INTERCONNECTEDNESS MEAN THAT AN AI CRASH COULD TRIGGER A BROAD AND DAMAGING STOCK MARKET CRASH 

Because a handful of tightly interconnected tech com-panies consume roughly half of the S&P 500’s market capitalization, a major fall in the value of AI-linked stocks would create a serious dent in the total value of the stock market even if all non-AI stocks remained unaffected. But a well-known economic adage is that in a crisis, all correla-tions go to one. That tendency for assets to fall together may be especially pronounced in the wake of an AI crash due to the sheer size of the AI boom. Several features of modern equity markets would threat-en to further spread and deepen any AI-driven stock market crash. The use of borrowed money, or leverage , to purchase and trade stocks is one well-known accelerant to market downturns. The best-known form of leverage is margin loans , in which a broker lends an investor mon-ey that the investor uses to buy stocks, bonds, or other securities. The securities in the investor’s portfolio serve as collateral for the margin loan, and margin accounts have credit limits tied to the value of those securities. The amount of margin debt investors are allowed to have thus goes up when the market rises and down when the market falls. During market downturns, investors who make heavy use of margin loans often face margin calls where the bro-ker requires the investor to either pay down the margin loan or post additional collateral to secure it. To comply with the margin call, investors often are forced to liqui-date parts of their portfolios. In a sharp downturn, many investors typically face margin calls at once, which creates a negative feedback loop if a large amount of margin debt has built up in the system: falling stock prices trigger mar-gin calls; to satisfy those margin calls, investors liquidate parts of their portfolios; this additional selling accelerates the downward slide of stock prices, which triggers more margin calls, and so on. These dynamics played out to devastating effect during the 1929 stock market crash. 204 42 

The total amount of outstanding margin loans hit a new all-time record of $1.5 trillion in June 2026 and remained just below that peak at the end of August, up 40% from just a year earlier and having more than doubled since ChatGPT’s debut. 205 While margin lending is substantially below its all-time peak as a percentage of total stock market capitalization, 206 it is at a record high in absolute terms and as a share of curren-cy in circulation 207 and GDP, 208 which increases the risk of collateral damage from a spate of margin calls. The rise of leveraged funds could further accelerate any market downturn. 209 Leveraged funds use a combination of derivatives and debt to return multiples of daily chang-es in the value of stock indices and, increasingly, in indi-vidual companies’ shares. While they still represent only a comparatively small share of the global equity market, leveraged funds have been growing rapidly in recent years and account for a disproportionate share of daily trad-ing. 210 Such funds gained attention during the July 2026 South Korean stock market crash, which leveraged funds accelerated and deepened. 211 An additional source of risk comes from the role of index funds in the modern stock market. Rather than invest-ing in stocks selected by a fund manager, index funds tie themselves to the collective performance of all stocks in a particular pre-determined index such as the S&P 500 or the tech-heavy NASDAQ-100. Because such funds move mechanistically with their assigned basket of stocks, they may increase market volatility and accentuate the market’s reflexive movements, making prices rise faster during booms but also fall more quickly during busts. 212 Today, more stocks are held in index funds and similar passive investment vehicles than at the time of any prior crash. 213 Taken together, these factors mean that any crash within the tech sector would not likely stay confined there. 

B. HOW AN AI CRASH COULD SPREAD TO THE FINANCIAL SYSTEM 

There are several potential pathways through which an AI crash could threaten the stability of the financial system. Private credit firms, many of which are already reeling from poor fund performance, hold hundreds of billions of dollars in risky AI-linked debt (Subsection 1). Life insurers likewise play a large and growing role in data center fi-nancing, and many have been purchased by private equity firms that have weakened insurers’ balance sheets (Sub-section 2). Both the private credit sector and life insurers have close ties to commercial banks; if panic grips either sector, the risk of contagion to the rest of the financial system would be high. These dangers are exacerbated by banks’ ties to the broader shadow banking system and their own holdings of AI-linked debt (Subsection 3).

If an AI-linked market crash were to occur, the private credit sector would find itself both heavily exposed to the

The private credit crisis 214 remained ongoing as this report went to press. The crisis has forced private investment firms to turn to increasingly speculative and risky tactics to avoid realizing losses.
