The private credit sector is staggering through these diffi-culties in large part because private credit is also playing a major role in financing data center construction, and that market, where interest rates are high, is still booming. 217 But if the market for AI data centers were to falter, the private credit crisis could easily spiral. As policymakers from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent 218 and Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman 219 to Senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal 220 have acknowledged, the poor transparency of private credit means that the sector occupies a regulatory blind spot. The opacity of private credit markets means that no one could be sure which funds (and the firms managing them) are solvent in a major crisis. Indeed, when transparency is poor, financial institutions may not even be sure of their own cash and financing needs, which can cause credit markets to freeze up, as happened with the markets tied to mortgage securities in 2007. 221 Up to now, financial regulations have insulated retail inves-tors and individual retirement accounts from direct exposure to ructions in private credit markets. The private investment industry has lobbied for years to change those regulations and gain access to the tens of trillions of dollars held in work-ers’ individual retirement accounts and 401(k)s. Unfortu-nately, they are finally on the verge of success: the Trump administration is moving to unlock the doors that have protected working people, retirees, and middle-class savers from opaque private capital markets. 222 While institutional investors have borne the brunt of private credit’s struggles thus far, individual workers and retirees could be increasingly and directly exposed going forward. The opacity of private credit also exposes the traditional banks on which our economy depends to a largely un-known slew of financial risks. The murky definition of private credit and the opacity of the private investment ecosystem make it difficult to estimate the exact amount of exposure of commercial banks to private credit, but, as of the first quarter of 2026, U.S. banks carried $2.7 tril-lion in exposures to nonbank lenders in the form of drawn and undrawn loan commitments. 223 Consequently, as New York Fed researchers found earlier this year, troubles from private lenders “result in ‘stress and strain’ for banks,” making the private credit ecosystem a potentially signifi-cant conduit through with an AI crash could spread to the banking system. 224 In a downturn, private credit funds and their portfolio companies may draw down bank credit lines precisely when the value of their assets is falling and other sources of financing are drying up. Banks could therefore experience a simultaneous increase in funding demands and deterioration in the quality of the collateral and counterparties supporting those demands. If banks respond by tightening lending standards, canceling credit lines, or otherwise making it harder to borrow, they could intensify the private credit downturn and transmit the strain of tightened credit to households and businesses with no direct connection to the AI industry. 

2. Mounting risks in the life insurance sector 

An AI crash or a deepening private credit crisis — and cer-tainly a combination of the two — would spell trouble for many life insurers, which fill key economic roles for both Main Street and Wall Street. For workers and consumers, life insurance is a way to access essential income in the case of catastrophic events. Increasingly, people have also turned to life insurers to provide them with annuities in retirement. For both traditional insurance and annuities, the purpose of life insurance is to provide a rock-solid guarantee of income for people when they need it most. Unfortunately, risky debt is becoming an increasingly central part of life insurers’ portfolios. Life insurers are now, to quote the Financial Times , the “lifeblood of private credit.” 225 About 20% of life insurers’ fixed-income assets are now tied to private and illiquid bonds, 226 and private credit holdings account for more than half of many life insurers’ fixed-income portfolios. 227 The intertwining of insurance and private credit is set to accelerate further, with 65% of U.S. insurers and 57% of insurers globally planning to invest more in private credit funds in the next 12 to 24 months. 228 44 

A growing number of life insurers have been purchased by private investment firms, including private credit giants like Apollo. This is deepening the tie-ups between life in-surers and the private credit sector. Life insurers owned by private investment firms are “gorging” on private credit, 229 including high-interest data center loans and purchases of phantom debt from BNPL firms. 230 Recent evidence suggests that insurers owned by private investment firms invest more money in illiquid, opaque, and high-yield (and thus high-risk) funds. 231 Such insurers also tend to be given the riskiest parts of private credit funds and buy identical assets at higher prices when the seller is another affiliate of the firm that owns the insurer. 232 At the same time, private investment firms are increas-ingly having the insurers they own purchase reinsurance through “captive reinsurers” controlled by the same pri-vate investment firm. Such captive reinsurers are usually established offshore in jurisdictions with poor transparen-cy laws, and many of the reinsurers appear to be invested in the same funds as the insurers. 233 That means a crash that threatens the solvency of a life insurer would also threaten the solvency of the reinsurer, which eliminates the whole purpose of reinsurance. While insurers owned by private equity firms appear uniquely exposed, independently owned and operated insurers appear to be taking on increasing levels of risky debt as well. The SEC is investigating ratings by the private credit ratings agency Egan Jones, which has rated $40 billion in insurer debt, with TIAA, MassMutual, and Principal Financial Group being among the biggest holders of debt rated by the agency. 234 Several life insurers have already taken major hits from the slow-rolling meltdown of the private credit market. 235 Life insurers are heavily involved in private lending to data center projects in particular and are increasingly exposed to AI-linked debt. 236 The opacity of these markets makes it, again, difficult to determine the amount of data center debt held by life insurers, but life insurers’ holdings of private and illiquid debt has spiked over the past few years, 237 and much of the recent growth in that debt has gone towards financing AI infrastructure, with life insurers “pouring capital into data center projects.” 238 This has led the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) to open an inquiry into whether the credit ratings underpinning insurers’ data center debt are justified. 239 Insurers’ role in data center financing is set to increase further, including through the purchases of private place-ment bonds. 240 The rapid growth in life insurers’ exposure to private credit in general and data center debt in particular means that an AI crash could have disastrous effects for many working-class people. There is a state-level guaranty system that pays the obligations of insolvent life insurance companies through assessments on surviving insurers in each state, but that system works slowly and has caps, making the failure of a life insurer devastating for its policyholders, particularly older Americans and their families and those who rely on annuities for economic security. Moreover, the structure of the guaranty system may make the U.S. life insurance sector more susceptible to contagion than is generally understood. 241 Under the guaranty system, surviving insurers are generally able to recoup any assessments through tax credits over five years, making the guaranty system an institutionalized form of publicly funded bailout. 242 Even leaving aside its dubiousness as a matter of policy, that bailout mechanism may not even be effective in a sharp crash that destabilizes several insurers at once — a distinct possibility in the case of an AI crash, given how widely AI-linked investments are held. If insurers already facing acute distress get hit with an assessment, the fact that they could eventually get that money back would be cold comfort. As explained in a recent article by legal scholars Pranjaj Drall and Andrew Granato, “[a] tipping point of distress exists where each wave of insolvencies would trigger assessments, in turn triggering further financial distress and contagion, and therefore another wave of insolvencies, creating a vicious cycle.” 243 Because 90 million American families rely on life insurance policies for financial security and retirement income, 244 a crisis in the life insurance sector would be an economic security disaster. Life insurers also play a key role in the financial system. Insurers have massive pools of long-term capital that are constantly replenished by the premiums paid by policy-holders. The biggest payments from life insurers, namely payouts after a policyholder dies, often happen decades after the policyholder starts paying premiums. This makes life insurers attractive counterparties for financial institu-tions that need short-term funding. 245 Insurers’ involve-ment in debt markets and extensive counterparty rela-tionships with other financial institutions is one reason the collapse of AIG posed a potential systemic risk during the 2008 financial crisis. Today, life insurers’ accumulation of opaque and illiquid assets means that they are becoming more likely to be a source of additional risk rather than a source of stability during a market crash. Consequently, serious contagion within the life insurance sector could quickly spread beyond it. 45 

3. Exposure of the banking system 

The most emergent phase of an economic crisis typically comes when financial institutions stop lending money. When credit markets freeze, as happened in August 2007 and (with even greater severity) September 2008, the basic plumbing of the modern financial system stops working. The exposure of life insurers and private credit funds to the AI sector, combined with the increased role of the shadow banking system — which includes private investment funds and insurers as well as other non-bank financial institutions such as hedge funds, mutual funds, and brokerages — means that many credit markets may be vulnerable even in the early stages of an AI crash. The worst effects on the real economy, however, come if a crisis reaches the banking system, which consists of commercial banks, credit unions, and other financial institutions that accept deposits from and lend money to the general public. Households and businesses rely on the banking system to pay their bills, meet payroll, and perform the other basic functions of the real economy. Today, banks are exposed to mounting risks both through their ties to the shadow banking system and through their own direct exposure to AI-linked debt. Commercial banks’ exposure to the shadow banking sys-tem has grown significantly since the 2008 financial crisis along with the shadow banking system itself. 246 A Federal Reserve report released in May 2026 noted that banks’ exposure to shadow debt was increasing quickly as of the end of 2025: 

Bank credit commitments to other financial entities grew appreciably in the fourth quarter of 2025 to $2.6 tril-lion, reflecting the growth in market-based finance and other forms of private nonbank lending. Private equity, BDCs [business development companies], and other private credit vehicles constituted the largest portion of bank lending to other financial entities. . . . Yearly growth of commitments has been notably robust for the special purpose entities, collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), and asset-backed securities category, followed by the other financial vehicles category and the private equity, BDCs, and private credit category. 247 

In other words, banks have rapidly expanding exposure to the shadow banking sector, and particularly to the types of opaque, complex, and risky shadow-system debt obligations that underpinned the last financial crisis — and that are increasingly prominent features of chip and data center financing arrangements. 248 Commercial banks also have considerable direct exposure to AI-linked debt. As the Abilene financing stack illus-trates, banks often sit at the base of data center financing structures. Although banks usually end up offloading most such syndicated loans to institutional investors, it can take several weeks or months for a bank to do so, particularly if demand for the loan ends up being less than anticipated. Moreover, banks typically keep some part of the debt on their balance sheets regardless. 249 Banks also had $450 billion in open commitments to AI-linked borrowers (primarily lines of credit) as of the end of 2025 of which $150 billion was outstanding. 250 The SEC’s loosening of rules on the securitization of data center debt means that AI-linked debt could become even more widely dispersed through the financial system. 251 None of these transmission routes — shadow banking, se-curitized debt, or banks’ direct lending to AI-linked com-panies — would necessarily be large enough, on its own, for an AI crash to seriously threaten the stability of the banking system. But together, they certainly could pose such a threat. Banks’ full exposure to both AI financing and the shadow banking sector may, moreover, be greater than is generally known. The systemic danger lies in how these risks interact. An AI downturn could reduce the value of loans held by private credit funds and insurers, leave banks stuck with loans they expected to sell, and trigger demands for additional bank funding. Funds and insurers under pressure could then sell similarly hard-to-trade assets, driving prices lower and causing further losses across the financial system. When credit markets deteriorate in this manner, banks typically respond by pulling back on lending, which can spark further defaults and drive cascading effects across the broader economy. Because these connections are often hidden in opaque private markets and off-balance-sheet arrange-ments, financial institutions may not be able to dependably assess their counterparties’ creditworthiness until funding dries up and credit markets begin to freeze. That is what happened in the 2007-2008 financial crisis: the extent to which the commercial and shadow banking systems were intertwined and exposed to the risky subprime market did not become apparent until credit markets froze and the entire financial system was in danger. 252 Moreover, as discussed further in Part IV, financial regula-tors have weakened many of the rules designed to protect banks from economic shocks. That leaves banks more vulnerable even as the risk of a crisis increases. 46 

C. DAMAGE TO THE REAL ECONOMY: NEGATIVE WEALTH EFFECTS AND IMPACTS ON WORKING FAMILIES 

The other forces that can cause asset crashes to spiral into economic crises play out over longer timescales than financial panics, but they can be just as devastating. Major asset crashes typically lead to recessions, as the bursting of the dot-com bubble did. Even recessions that never result in systemic financial crises have devastating effects on workers’ and consumers’ economic security, particular-ly workers who are laid off and older workers and retirees whose pension plans collapse in value. And just as finan-cial crises often trigger recessions, severe recessions can eventually lead to financial crises as the effects of falling wages and asset prices spread through the economy. The negative wealth effect represents one key mechanism through which damage from falling asset prices propa-gates. As its name implies, the negative wealth effect is the inverse of the wealth effect , which takes hold when people see the value of their assets increase. This makes them feel wealthier, which spurs them to spend more money. Some of the additional spending goes towards purchasing additional or more valuable financial assets, such as stocks or real estate. The additional demand for those assets pushes their value even higher, which in-creases people’s wealth still further. At the same time, the additional wealth means people have more money to spend on consumer goods, whether by selling some of their assets or by using those assets as collateral to obtain credit from banks. The resulting increased consumption of goods boosts corporate profits, which makes stocks ap-pear even more attractive. The wealth effect thus acts as a force multiplier in good times, creating virtuous cycles that accelerate the economy’s upward trajectory. 253 But the same forces that propel the economy up in boom times can just as easily drag it down. When people see the value of their houses, stocks, or other assets fall, they start to feel less wealthy, causing them to pull back on spend-ing. In a deep enough downturn, people may be forced to sell assets just to cover their bills, especially if they took on too much debt during the boom times. People find it harder to obtain loans, which further cuts consumption. These forces cause asset prices to fall even more, which lowers people’s wealth even further in a self-reinforcing negative feedback loop — the negative wealth effect. Similar forces can take hold even if the amount of wealth destroyed in an asset crash is relatively small. When falling asset prices create uncertainty about economic condi-tions, consumers may cut back on spending even if their net worth remains relatively unchanged. This is one reason why the Great Crash of 1929 led to a broad and prolonged drop in consumer spending even though relatively few Americans owned stock at the time — the crash shook confidence in the economy, which led even consumers who did not hold stock to cut back on spending. 254 The negative wealth effects of a stock market crash today could be severe because such a crash would destroy a previously unthinkable amount of wealth at a time when consumers already have a negative view of the economy. With $76 trillion in publicly traded equities representing nearly 240% of GDP as of September 2026, the stock market is much bigger today, both in absolute terms and relative to the economy as a whole, than it was in 1929 or, indeed, at the time of any prior crash. 255 Consequently, as the Bank of International Settlements’ 2026 Annual Eco-nomic Report warns, “[a] major equity market correction could have larger macroeconomic consequences today than in the past,” with severe consequences for global financial stability. 256 Because of Big Tech’s dominance of those equity markets, even a 25% drop in the value of the Magnificent Seven — just enough to take them back to roughly where they were in May 2025 — would wipe out over $5 trillion in paper wealth, more than the GDP of the United King-dom. If U.S. stock markets were to fall by 45%, taking them back to the levels they were shortly before the re-lease of ChatGPT, it would evaporate $35 trillion — more than the entire U.S. economy produces in a year. And that is not even the worst-case scenario. Recall that the stock market is historically overvalued, with the S&P 500 having a CAPE ratio of 42, roughly two and a half times its long-run average of 17. If stock prices fell just to that historical average, $45 trillion in paper wealth would vanish. Needless to say, if prices were to drop below that historical average — as often happens during economic crises 257 — the wealth destruction would be worse still. The negative wealth effects of an AI crash would likely be amplified still further by the historically high level of income inequality. As Galbraith noted in The Great Crash ,a “bad distribution of income” was a key reason the econ-omy was unable to regain its footing after 1929: 

Th[e] highly unequal income distribution meant that the economy was dependent on a high level of investment or a high level of luxury consumer spending or both. The rich cannot buy great quantities of bread. If they are to 47 

dispose of what they receive, it must be on luxuries or by way of investment in new plants and new projects. . . . This high-bracket spending and investment was espe-cially susceptible, one may assume, to the crushing news from the stock market in October of 1929. 258 

Income inequality today is similarly extreme, 259 and consumer spending is disproportionately driven by the highest earners, who are also the ones who would lose the most if the stock market plummets. 260 The wealth effect from rising stock prices drove an additional $250 billion in increased consumer spending in the United States be-tween the summers of 2024 and 2025. 261 The flip side of that coin is that consumer spending could fall dramatically in a serious market downturn. The K-shaped economy of recent years thus serves as an additional source of poten-tial systemic risk. But it is not only the wealthy who would suffer. The stock ownership rate is far higher today than it was in 1929, and a record number of working-class Americans own stock, primarily through retirement accounts and pen-sion funds. 262 As major holders of risky unsecured data center debt, pension funds would be among the first hit if a significant amount of data center debt became toxic, according to a recent analysis by Stefan Hepp of the Uni-versity of Chicago’s Booth School of Business. 263 These losses would hit pension funds hard, particularly since AI-linked assets dominate stock and corporate bond markets as well. 264 Pension funds are also becoming ever-more exposed to risky private credit debt even as that sector comes under strain. 265 Big Tech’s dominance of stock markets also means that workers’ retirement accounts would be hit hard in an AI crash, particularly after SpaceX pressured executives of the world’s largest stock index providers to change their inclusion rules to get itself fast-tracked into Nasdaq, FTSE Russell, and CRSP. 266 In pushing for the rule chang-es, SpaceX engineered a stock market in which retirement savers invested in passive funds tracking those indices would be forced to buy the highly volatile stock whether they wanted to or not. The Trump administration’s move to open retirement accounts to private capital markets could further transfer AI risk to workers’ retirement accounts. 267 The increasing risks to pension funds and retirement accounts mean that older workers and retirees would be especially hard-hit by a stock market crash. Other working families would be affected as well. Workers ex-periencing unemployment or pay cuts after a crash could be forced to liquidate their retirement accounts to pay living expenses. The rising amount of risky consumer debt creates a further risk that consumer spending could fall quickly in an economic downturn. All these forces would further intensify the negative wealth effect. It may not take much for a negative wealth effect to take hold. Ordinary Americans already have a historically neg-ative view of the economy, with consumer sentiment at an all-time low despite the rising stock market. 268 A falling stock market would likely send consumer confidence plummeting still further, reducing spending and amplify-ing downward pressures on the real economy. 

D. FALLING INVESTMENT AND STRANDED ASSETS COULD WEIGH DOWN THE ECONOMY 

The outlook for the American economy in the wake of an AI-driven crash could be especially bleak due to the effects of falling investment and stranded assets. Falling asset prices cause investment to fall along with spend-ing, thus starving the economy of a key fuel that drives growth. As with the negative wealth effect, this can create a negative feedback loop. Falling stock prices cause investment to decline; declining investment hurts pro-ductivity and economic growth, which pushes corporate earnings down further, which causes stock prices to fall further, and so on. The massive physical footprint of the AI data center buildout and the amount of debt tied up in it means that the bursting of the AI bubble could make investment fall especially quickly. This factor would come into play with particular force if an AI crash results from (or results in) a stagnation or decline in generative AI sales, whether due to a dropoff in overall demand or users simply declining to pay for more expen-sive models. This would not be a major problem if AI chips and data centers could simply be used for non-AI work-loads. That may not be economical, however, because AI chips have significantly higher power and cooling require-ments — and thus are more expensive to operate — than the chips used for traditional cloud computing. 269 More-over, the power and cooling needs for AI training are more intense than those used for AI inference. 270 Repurposing AI data centers thus could be economically challenging. 271 If expected AI demand fails to materialize and the cost of powering and cooling highly specialized AI chips and data centers turns out to be greater than whatever economic value companies can extract from those assets, the eco-nomically rational course would be to abandon them. Such 

stranded assets destroy economic value, particularly if 48 

they have debt attached to them; a company may save on operational costs by letting a data center go dark, but any obligations associated with the data center would remain. As Advait Arun wrote in Bubble or Nothing, a report by the Center for Public Enterprise, the bursting of the AI bubble could leave behind a range of stranded assets: “Not only does a prospective market correction create potential stranded assets of data centers, which will lose value as their lease revenue disappears, but it threatens to strand all the energy projects and efficiency innovations that data center demand might have called forth.” 272 In such a case, abandoned data centers and connected in-frastructure could be white elephants to the communities where they are located — a particularly bitter outcome since many state and local governments gave tax incen-tives to the data center developers to attract them. 273 The comparatively short lifespan of AI chips also means that even the assets that retain their value initially probably would not have a long tail of productive use. Even ignoring the likelihood of technological obsolescence, AI chips’ useful life appears to be well under ten years. The hyperscalers’ balance sheets claim their chips last five to six years, and one analysis found that a cohort of AI GPUs with an expected life of 5.5 years was trending towards an actual life of just 3.7 years based on real world use. 274 Top data center GPUs may last just 1-3 years with typical utilization. 275 The lifespan of AI chips thus appears to be at least an order of magnitude less than fiber-optic cable, the main capex focus during the dot-com boom, which has a lifespan of several decades or more; some of the earliest fiber lines laid in the 1980s remain in active use today. 276 Railroads likewise have a lifespan of many decades. 277 The high operating costs and short lifespans of AI assets mean that, in the wake of an AI downturn, there is a high risk that stranded assets would act as a further drag on economic growth. This would create a risk of a bal-ance-sheet recession similar to the one that led to Japan’s “Lost Decade” in the 1990s, when economic growth ground to a halt as businesses, financial institutions, and investors spent years clearing bad loans and underwater assets from their balance sheets. 278 

E. SURVEYING THE MINEFIELD: WHY NAVIGATING THE FALLOUT FROM AN AI CRASH WOULD BE DIFFICULT 

The rising danger of an economic crisis comes not from any one factor. Rather, it comes from the fact that the economy may well have to navigate all of these sources of instability (including those that this report has bare-ly touched on, such as the rapid rise in risky consumer debt, pressure from rising interest rates, and the vola-tile multi-trillion-dollar cryptocurrency market) in the aftermath of an AI crash. Navigating the fallout from an AI crash would be akin to maneuvering through a dense minefield, knowing that one wrong step could not only cause serious damage on its own, but potentially set off a chain reaction. The delicate task of navigating these accumulating risks would be extremely difficult even for the most vigilant and competent regulators and policymakers under the best of circumstances. In past crises, the Federal Reserve has served as a “lender of last resort” to stop economic crises from spiraling out of control while the Treasury Department and other federal agencies and officials played an essential role in calming stormy markets. But the tools in the Fed’s crisis management toolkit may be less effective in the face of an AI crash, and the Trump Administration has hardly instilled confidence that it would be a source of calm and stability in a resulting crisis. Historically, investors have flocked to purchase U.S. treasuries and scoop up dollars as safe havens in times of instability. Strong demand for dollars and treasuries makes it cheaper for the federal government to borrow money (essential for economic stimulus) and easier for the Fed to print new dollars to inject liquidity into shaky markets. But when markets destabilized in the wake of the Trump administration’s “Liberation Day” tariff announcement, treasury yields rose and the dollar fell — a stunning re-versal of the market’s usual response to crises. 279 Markets stabilized after the Trump administration backtracked, but the incident suggested that investors may no longer rush to buy up American assets if the U.S. economy sustains self-inflicted wounds. Sure enough, during the Iran War, there were signs that a growing number of investors viewed Chinese bonds as the safer bet. 280 As of Septem-ber 2026, long-dated U.S. Treasury bond yields are at their highest levels since the height of the mid-2000s housing bubble (when benchmark interest rates were significantly higher), indicating that, despite the booming stock market and high levels of investment, investors are already nervous about the federal government’s ability to cover its debts. 281 When Secretary Bessent announced an expansion of treasury bond buybacks in August in an attempt to bring rates down, yields fell only briefly before rebounding to elevated levels. 282 49 

In a crisis arising from the core of the U.S. economy, and particularly one where the U.S. economy looks likely to be weighed down by stranded assets, investors may prove distinctly less eager to buy U.S. treasuries or hold their reserves in U.S. dollars. Other countries’ monetary and fiscal policy chiefs may also be wary of coordinating with the Trump Administra-tion, which has disdained cooperation through multilateral institutions. Central bankers and finance ministers know that the current crop of U.S. treasury officials is behold-en to the whims of a volatile president who has shown a marked tendency to renege on economic agreements. Summits of the G7 and G20, which played a key role in coordinating the responses to the financial crises of 1997 and 2008, seem much less likely to bear fruit if a crisis arises in the next two-plus years. A dangerous AI crash is not inevitable, nor are the econ-omy-wrecking consequences that could follow. But at-tention and policy action are urgently required to contain the risks and prevent any potential crisis from devastating millions of people’s lives and livelihoods. Federal regulators, Congress, state officials, and private standard-setting bodies each have a role to play in cracking down on these activities, which can mislead investors and have repeatedly characterized speculative bubbles in recent decades. The SEC should proactively investigate credible inves-tor allegations of deceptive revenue reporting practices, failure to disclose certain existing or planned debt ar-rangements or issuances, knowingly issuing unreliably high revenue projections, and other similarly deceptive, fraudulent, and/or unfair activities. The PCAOB, which is overseen by the SEC, should likewise scrutinize the tech-niques AI companies are using to keep multi-billion-dollar financial commitments off their balance sheets and direct inspectors to conduct detailed compliance reviews across large auditing firms with a focus on those firms’ data center- and AI-related clients. Those found to be out of compliance should face enforcement action. The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB), a pri-vate standard-setting body, should publish data it is cur-rently collecting on data infrastructure projects and pri-vate credit-sponsored vehicles. At the same time, FASB should issue guidance clarifying what can be considered a “reasonable and supportable” useful life estimate for GPUs. It should also move swiftly to formally strengthen standards for determining when a variable interest entity (VIE , a category inclusive of SPVs) must be included on companies’ balance sheets. The repeated and escalating use of deceptive tactics to mislead investors and pensioners suggests that statutory changes are needed. As Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator’s Asad Ramzanali has argued, 311 Congress should prohibit large-scale circular equity financing deals, large-scale debt financing deals whose ultimate capital sources are undisclosed, and the use of SPVs and similar vehicles to avoid disclosing debt-like obligations in companies’ public financial reports. State regulators and law enforcement officials should use their authorities under anti-fraud and accountancy laws 312 to investigate and, where appropriate, prosecute com-panies and executives where they have used or approved fraudulent financial practices. There are several past examples of regulators and attorneys general using these corporate accountability tools as firms were falling apart under the weight of their mismanagement, including in the aftermath of the dot-com crash. The successful state enforcement action against Arthur Andersen in the after-math of the Enron scandal serves as a particularly strong model in this regard (see inset). 

The Texas State Board of Public Accountancy (TSBPA) successfully prosecuted onetime auditing giant Arthur Andersen, then one of the largest accounting firms in the world, for its role in the Enron scandal. The TSBPA ultimately found that Andersen had “failed to follow generally accepted auditing standards and generally ac-cepted accounting principles in attest work it performed for Enron between 1997 and 2002,” and that the firm “lacked objectivity, integrity, and independence” in its role as Enron’s external auditor. In particular, the TSBPA underscored that, during those years, Enron’s financial statements were “materially misstated, in part because the company used certain ‘special purpose entities’ to record debt that should have been booked to Enron’s financial statements.” In August 2002, the TSBPA revoked Andersen’s CPA licensing, and the firm ceased operations. 313 

State law enforcement officials also brought enforcement actions against financial institutions that recommended that investors buy dot-com stocks and debt issued by their corporate clients, even as they privately described those offerings as junk. Observers have identified similari-ties between that episode and today’s IPO frenzy. 314 This time policymakers should not wait until after the crisis arrives to act. They should move proactively to investigate dubious practices and, where firms or individu-als are breaking the law, bring enforcement actions. State securities regulators can use their authorities to protect investors by investigating and referring to the relevant bodies credible fraud claims alleged by investors under their jurisdiction. Already, state securities regulators are pursuing investiga-tions into and enforcement actions against fraudsters who “imply that artificial intelligence is being used to improve the success of the investment.” 315 Such actions correctly signal that slapping the term “artificial intelligence” on an offering is not an incantation that shields securities issuers from the law. These so-called AI-washing cases have largely focused on companies accused of misrepresenting their use of AI technologies as a means of boosting their 56 

share price and attracting investor interest. However, AI firms that mislead the public and/or investors regarding the development, capabilities, and challenges of their models, the nature of their financial position, or other material matters (as investors recently accused Google of doing in its communications regarding the rollout of Gemini 3.5) 316 may also be violating securities laws. If so, federal and state securities regulators should hold firms accountable. 

d. Halt AI-related risk transfers to working people and stop subsidizing the bubble with public funds 

The inflation of the AI bubble is being fed by private sector actions and policy decisions that make it easier to offload the risks of AI development onto working people and that subsidize AI activity, whether directly through tax breaks or through exemptions and exceptions that give special favors to AI companies. Policymakers should stop these giveaways and limit the damage. Powerful index providers like Nasdaq have aided in this risk transfer by accelerating the addition of new stocks — already those issued by SpaceX, and perhaps those of Anthropic and OpenAI next — to their indices. Fast-tracked index inclusion means that retail investors and retirement savers’ portfolios are being saddled with these AI-related shares, whether they want them or not, at inflated post-IPO prices. And, just as everyday investors are forced into these AI investments, wealthy insiders are able to sell their shares for the first time in a market with built-in demand. Policymakers in Congress and elsewhere can and should investigate how and why NASDAQ and other exchanges made the decision to accelerate index inclusion for these large, newly public companies. Moreover, because fast-tracked inclusions, financial opacity, and circular funding permeate the AI industry, policymakers and courts should make it clear that fiduciaries’ obligations require them to actively consider whether these new stocks belong in index funds and whether investments in index funds that do include them can be made in a manner consistent with fiduciary duties. 317 Massive sales of risky AI investments to pension funds represent another pathway through which working fam-ilies are being exposed to the dangers of the AI bubble. Pension fund decisionmakers have fiduciary obligations to act prudently, including by asking tough questions about what they are being sold and avoiding conflicts of inter-est. 318 Policymakers must support those decisionmakers by requiring transparency, engaging in oversight, and preventing fraudulent and deceptive practices. A recent letter from the AFT to Treasury Secretary Bessent pro-vides a useful guide to needed steps. 319 AI companies are also effectively offloading risk onto life insurance policyholders by tapping their premiums as a funding source. B. PRINCIPLES FOR FACING THE ACUTE PHASE OF AN AI CRASH 

If faced with an AI-induced financial crisis and severe economic downturn, policymakers must depart from the unjust and moral-hazard-inducing playbooks of the past. Policymakers must reject bailouts for failing AI companies, financial institutions, and/or the billionaires who own and run them (Subsection 1). Instead, crisis response should be focused on stabilization and recovery efforts that prioritize working people and families rather than imposing auster-ity measures that force workers and consumers to bear the brunt of the resulting economic pain (Subsection 2). Corporations and executives that engaged in fraudulent, deceptive, or other unlawful acts must be held accountable (Subsection 3). 

1. No billionaire bailouts 

AI companies and the financial companies serving them have inflated the valuations of their businesses, made big bets based on billionaires’ wild projections, and loaded the financial system with trillions of dollars in speculative debt, generating enormous wealth for themselves while creating serious dangers for everyone else. They know what they are doing is risky; in apparent anticipation of the company’s possible need for a bailout, OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar floated the idea of a government “backstop” for the company back in November of 2025. 323 In the face of acute AI industry stress, Congress and executive branch officials must steadfastly oppose bailouts to prop up embattled industry actors or protect them from facing the financial or legal consequences of their actions. Federal policymakers must reject any proposal to rescue AI firms or their executives or financiers with pub-lic funds, including through stimulus funds, lines of credit, grants, tax abatements, rescue funding, golden shares, purchases of distressed assets, and/or the unconditional or lightly conditioned use of Fed emergency facilities. In addition to being the right thing to do, committing to a no-bailouts policy now would deter further reckless lend-ing and speculative investment, thus reducing both the likelihood and potential severity of an AI crash. 

No Big Tech bailouts 

If they face collapse, neither AI-related firms nor their leadership should be shielded from the financial or legal consequences of their mismanagement. Under no circum-stances should failing AI-related firms receive government support to remain going concerns. Instead, failed AI firms should be moved through legal proceedings for liquidating and/or dissolving firms in an orderly manner. As discussed in No Bailouts for Big Tech Billionaires , AI companies themselves are not systemically important in the same way that megabanks are: 

None of the Magnificent Seven, the neoclouds, or AI startups hold the money that consumers use to pay bills, lend money to small businesses, or hold billions of dollars of each other’s liquid assets. There simply is no reason a tech company, even a historically large one, cannot go through the usual bankruptcy process .324 58 

While imperfect, the U.S. bankruptcy process is designed to safely wind up failing companies while securing as much value as possible for small businesses, consumers, and other harmed creditors. That said, too often, wealthy corporate insiders have abused the bankruptcy process to divert dying firms’ resources to themselves. Moreover, several of the hyperscalers have access to vast troves of personal data that should not simply be sold off to the highest bidder. Consequently, any Big Tech bankruptcy process must be administered in a manner that removes corporate executives and insiders from their positions and holds them accountable, provides for robust clawbacks of pre-bankruptcy compensation and shareholder distri-butions, and provides strong protections for consumers, workers, and communities. While available to bankruptcy judges and trustees, such provisions should be standard practice in large Chapter 7 and 11 bankruptcies. Congress can and should pass legislation to set that standard. If government intervention is required to ensure essen-tial cloud, digital, and/or other infrastructure continues functioning, the federal government should acquire that infrastructure at no more than market prices — which, in a deep enough crash, may well be close to zero. To facil-itate the continued operation of critical infrastructure, the federal government should take relevant corporate entities into a receivership structure under which corpo-rate executives are removed, crucial staff are retained, and functions critical to the economy are carried out, similar to the FDIC’s framework for operating a “bridge bank” after certain commercial banks fail. 325 Ultimately, critical digital infrastructure should be subject to a regulatory regime that guarantees its operation benefits the public, as discussed in the Open Markets Institute’s 2025 report, 

Engineering the Cloud Commons .326 

No bailouts for Wall Street 

Likewise, there should be no bailouts for failing financial firms or federal backstops that shield big banks, private investment funds, wealthy insider investors, and other bubble financiers from losses. Instead, insolvent banks should be moved into the FDIC’s orderly resolution process, which was designed after the last financial crisis to “protect insured depositors, preserve value, promote financial stability, and prevent taxpayer bailouts.” 327 If a rapid and orderly resolution under ordi-nary insolvency regimes is not possible — a scenario quite likely to unfold if a systemically important bank fails — the FDIC can act through its statutory authority under Title II of the Dodd-Frank Act. Title II provides the FDIC with tools to “mitigate risks to financial stability by providing for the appointment of the FDIC as receiver of a failed financial company and for an Orderly Liquidation Fund (OLF) to serve as a temporary backstop source of liquid-ity.” 328 Neither of these resolution frameworks require or even contemplate the use of publicly funded bailouts. Our focus here on existing bank resolution frameworks is not to suggest that we believe these frameworks are perfect — they aren’t. But regulators must make use of the tools they have. Otherwise, history demonstrates that ad hoc bailouts repeatedly benefit wealthy insiders at the expense of everyone else. Such bailouts undermine faith in democratic institutions and encourage the sort of excessive risk-taking that sows the seeds for future crises, particularly when they benefit people whose poor lending, borrowing, investment, or management decisions helped create the crisis in the first place. When Citigroup faced significant stress in 2008, for exam-ple, the FDIC used a systemic risk exception to guarantee $306 billion in assets held by the bank. Citigroup was, of course, facing such significant stress in part because it had engaged in corporate accounting fraud and predatory lending practices in the years preceding the crash, harming everyday investors and consumers in the process. 329 During the same period, the FDIC used the exception to offer a $118 billion asset guarantee to Bank of America in “antici-pation of market pressure” on the bank. 330 Bank of America, too, had violated securities laws and engaged in predatory lending practices in the two years leading up to the 2008 crash. 331 But households and communities – many of which were directly harmed by these and other banks’ deceptive and fraudulent actions – did not receive federal aid granted in “anticipation of market pressure.” Over the course of the following decade, working people would face mass unem-ployment and sweeping housing foreclosures. Entire cities would lose most of their tax bases, with systemic disinvest-ment taking a devastating toll on working families. Financial regulators followed a similar playbook in 2023 during the failures of the crypto-linked banks discussed in Part I.B.2. When Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) and Signa-ture Bank collapsed, the FDIC invoked the systemic risk exception and used its Deposit Insurance Fund (DIF) to cover tens of billions in uninsured deposits held by wealthy clients, venture capital firms, and tech companies. That left the FDIC on the hook for $20 billion in losses, which are borne in part by consumers in the form of bank fees. Meanwhile, SVB’s former CEO was flying first class to Hawai ʻi and hanging on to the nearly $10 million he’d been paid the previous year while mismanaging the bank. 59 

The federal response to the next financial crisis must avoid the unjust and unjustified bailouts of the past. 

2. Stabilizing the economy by supporting Main Street 

No corporate bailouts does not mean no action. To minimize the severity and breadth of a crisis, policymak-ers should focus their efforts on supporting the workers, consumers, retirees, and communities whose economic security would be at stake in a crisis. Such efforts will both reduce the immediate harms and make for a swifter and more equitable recovery. The federal response to an AI bubble-induced crisis should prioritize preserving basic economic security and provid-ing people with access to housing, healthcare, nutrition assistance, elder- and childcare. For those who suffer job losses, the federal government should move quickly to make enhanced unemployment insurance available and lower the likelihood of a sustained drop in household consumption. Steps like these will both limit the economic pain experienced by families and reduce the potential im-pact of the negative wealth effects discussed in Part III.C. In a crisis triggered by a bursting AI bubble — and giv-en the multiple channels through which Wall Street is exposing working people to AI-related financial risks — the federal government must also address the needs of modest investors reliant on their retirement accounts for economic security in the immediate term as well as working people and retirees whose pensions face major AI-related losses. In the event of a crisis, state and local governments are also likely to be squeezed by economic contraction. They may also face an additional set of challenges unique to the AI bubble, as abandoned data center projects and tax subsidies provided to their developers could further constrain economic recovery. It will be crucial that the federal government provide state and local governments with the financial support necessary to continue delivering core services, in addition to the funding those govern-ments already receive for health care, housing, nutrition, and other needs. 

3. Hold wrongdoers accountable 

Where firms or individuals are found to have broken the law, they must be held accountable. The failure to pur-sue wrongdoers was one of the most noteworthy failures of the response to the subprime mortgage bubble and the crash that followed. Despite well-documented fraud ranging from mortgage lenders systemically altering loan paperwork to bankers knowingly ripping off their own clients to get out from bad bets, 332 no executive of any of the largest financial institutions involved was held crimi-nally liable for their misconduct. Civil and administrative enforcement actions were little stronger, with Wall Street banks receiving far more in bailouts than in fines. That lack of accountability played a significant role in damaging the public’s faith in democratic institutions. As described earlier in this report, deceptive practices are playing an essential role in inflating and maintaining the AI bubble. Where law enforcement officials and/or regulators identify unlawful practices that have harmed the public, investors, or consumers, the executives and high-level managers who directed and executed the unlawful con-duct should be held accountable. Fiduciaries who failed to fulfill their obligations to pension plan participants or fund investors should also be held accountable. 

C. BUILDING A MORE RESILIENT FINANCIAL SYSTEM FOR THE MANY 

This report has focused on exposing the dangers of an AI crash and financial crisis and describing steps that policy-makers can and should take to mitigate potential harms. Much broader structural reforms are required to better tame the cycle of speculative bubbles that enrich insiders, harm millions of people when they burst, and concentrate economic and political power at the top. A fulsome exploration of those reforms is beyond this re-port’s scope, but the need for such broader reforms is one of its central lessons. Our analysis here points to some key principles for the needed changes in finance, which we very briefly outline here: • Policymakers must adopt tough financial transparency, accounting, and auditing standards that prevent dangerous financial engineering, and hold all parties accountable when they fail to comply with their legal obligations. • Policymakers must establish a robust regulatory floor for the shadow banking sector that subjects such firms to strong supervisory, consumer protection, and disclosure regimes and therefore disincentivizes regulatory arbitrage. • Policymakers must provide investors, workers, and consumers with tools that grant them power over corporate decision-making processes and enable them to hold corporate insiders accountable. 60 

• Policymakers must update the framework for bank regulation and hold the financial system and individual financial institutions to far higher standards for resilience. The severe consequences of bank failures are a product of the critical role banks play in the economy; the danger of an AI crash becoming a systemic financial crisis is increased by banks’ growing entanglement with non-bank financial companies. Banks — especially large ones — receive high levels of government support in the operation of their businesses. Consistent with that government support, and given their critical role, new and much higher standards that require banks to focus on serving the public interest are needed. 333 Lasting reform will, of course, require much more than simply addressing the most obvious features of the current bubble and its most recent predecessors. It will require shifting the rules of the financial system so that it better supports the movement of capital towards pro-ductive and sustainable ends, is significantly less prone to dangerous boom and bust cycles, and guarantees eco-nomic security for all while providing communities the opportunity to flourish. Achieving those goals will require reforms to expand the power of workers, consumers, and communities while limiting the economic and political power of corporations. It will also require restructuring the financial system so that it serves the needs of the real economy rather than the other way around. The ability of working people to retire in comfort must be secured through robust protec-tions for retirement savers and income support for all ag-ing people. Security in retirement must be less dependent on the short-term whims of the market. Workers’ savings should not be treated as a pool of capital for Wall Street to use to its maximum advantage. Last but certainly not least, true reform will also mean ensuring that billionaires and large corporations cannot accumulate the economic and political power that enables them to create economy-threatening bubbles in the first place. 61

# Conclusion 

# Toward the end of The Great Crash , Galbraith called policymakers’ response to the 1929 crash a “triumph of dogma over thought.” In the summer of 1929, the Federal Reserve had meekly asked the banks to stop fueling the speculative frenzy but, having largely been captured in personnel and entirely captured in thought by Wall Street, refused to go any further. After the crash came, policymakers continued to blunder, stubbornly hewing to conventional laissez-faire wisdom by cutting spending when demand was plummeting and obsessing over preventing inflation even as the air was seeping out of the economy. They persisted in this approach even though logic and a mounting pile of evidence suggested that they were worried about all the wrong things, exemplifying the “poor state of economic intelligence” that Galbraith highlighted as a key factor contributing to the economy’s eventual spiral into the Great Depression. Nearly a century later, another major crisis is brewing. With a yawning and still-widening gap between revenues and spending, the AI industry’s financial position is becoming increasingly precarious. It may soon become untenable, if it has not already. But a disastrously severe crash is not, or at least not yet, an inevitable outcome. If they act swiftly and decisively, policymakers can reduce the AI bubble’s threat to working people, communities, and the broader economy by slowing the bubble’s inflation, shining a light on the true health of the AI industry’s finances, and halting the transfer of AI-related financial risk to working people and everyday investors. They must also use and bolster the regulatory guardrails that make the financial institutions on which the real economy depends more resilient in the face of stress. These steps would lessen the danger of an AI crash cascading into an unmanageable economic crisis. Unfortunately, financial regulators appear too captured both by Wall Street and Silicon Valley’s market power and by AI hype to recognize, much less contend with, the fast-mounting risks. By moving to lower capital requirements, expose 401(k)s to private markets, and reduce financial transparency, the Trump administration and the Federal Reserve are making risk more attractive and debt more easily accessible even as speculation runs rampant. In so doing, they are leaving workers and consumers more exposed to a crash rather than less. Time for decisive action is running short. If dogma triumphs over thought again, future historians may need to ask for clarification when someone mentions the Great Crash. 63

# Glossary of Terms AI Chip Specialized computer processing chips that perform the intensive computation required to train and run generative AI models. Includes Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) and Google/ Broadcom tensor processing units (TPUs). 

Artificial intelligence (AI) 

A computational system trained on data to recognize patterns, make predictions, or generate outputs such as text, images, audio, and video. Because nearly all of the debt and spending in the AI bubble is on generative AI infrastructure, references to “AI” should be assumed to refer to generative AI unless otherwise specified. 

Commoditization The process where intense competition, low barriers to entry, or other factors create a low-margin market consisting of several companies offering interchangeable goods or services. 

Depreciation A common but easily abused accounting method where the cost of an asset is spread over the asset’s useful life rather than booked all at once. 

Generative AI AI systems that generate text, images, or other output in response to an inquiry or prompt. 

Graphics processing unit (GPU) 

The specialized class of computer processing chips most commonly used to train and often to run generative AI models. Used interchangeably with “AI chips” in this report. 

Hyperscaler The corporations, all based in the U.S., that are spending the most money on building AI infrastructure. Most commonly refers to Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Oracle, and sometimes CoreWeave and SpaceX as well. 

Index fund An investment vehicle where investors purchase shares in a fund that tracks the value of a specific index, such as the S&P 500. 

Inference The stage where a trained AI model generates outputs (such as text, answers, or predictions) in response to user inputs. 

Large language model (LLM) 

The subtype of generative AI that powers ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and other text-based generative AI chatbots and related products. 

Leverage Generic financial term referring to the use of borrowed money to invest in or purchase assets. 

Leveraged fund Exchange-traded or mutual funds that use debt and derivatives to deliver multiples of the daily changes in the value of a stock, index fund, or other security. 

Margin call A demand by a lender that the borrower provide additional collateral, typically because the value of the borrower’s existing collateral has deteriorated. Margin calls frequently happen for margin debt accounts during sharp stock market downturns. 

Margin debt / margin loan 

Money that a broker has loaned to an investor for the purchase of stock, bonds, or other securities. 

Model developer A corporation or other organization that develops LLMs or other generative AI models and offers related products and services to the public. 87 

Model training The process through which a generative AI system identifies patterns from data and uses those patterns to produce new outputs. 

Negative wealth effect Negative feedback loop where falling wealth leads people to cut spending, which hurts economic growth. Inverse of the wealth effect. 

Neocloud Companies (e.g., CoreWeave and Nebius) that focus on developing data centers and leasing access to AI chips to generative AI model developers. 

Private investment firm Non-bank financial institutions that manage private credit or private equity funds. 

Private credit Loans and other forms of debt provided outside traditional bank lending and bond markets. Most often, they are issued by non-bank financial institutions and not traded on public credit markets. 

Private equity Shares and equity in privately held companies that are not traded on public stock markets, or the firms that specialize in managing investment funds that generate profits from the purchase of such equity. 

Round-tripping Deceptive financial arrangement where two companies exchange the same money, goods, or other assets back and forth to create the false appearance of real revenue even though no real economic value is created. 

Securitization The process of pooling loans or other debt obligations into a tradeable bond or similar security, the cash flows from which (e.g., interest payments on the underlying loans) are effectively sold to investors. 

Shadow banking system The system of non-bank financial institutions such as private investment firms, hedge funds, insurers, mutual funds, that manage assets, lend money, and engage in other bank-like functions but that operate outside the regulatory system that governs banks and similar depository institutions like credit unions. 

Special-purpose vehicle (SPV) 

A shell company set up by a sponsor corporation that holds specific assets or liabilities, often in order to keep those assets and liabilities off the sponsoring corporation’s books. 

Stranded asset An asset that loses its economic value before the end of its functional or operational life. Can occur if the asset becomes obsolete or costs more to operate than it can generate in revenue. 

Token The fragments of text that LLMs process and generate. Billing for generative AI products/services is increasingly done on a per-token basis. 

Understating depreciation 

Dubious accounting tactic where a company effectively claims that an asset has a longer useful life than it actually does, thus allowing the company to spread the cost of the asset over a longer period of time on its balance sheet and make its current expenses appear artificially low. 

Wealth effect Positive feedback loop where wealthier people spend more and stimulate economic growth. Inverse of the negative wealth effect. 88
